en: *Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Mahāyāna Master Ji. I.

Manifesting the Causes for its Arising; II. Announcing the Year of Composition; III. Explaining the Main Text. Regarding the first [section], there are two parts. First: [The text continues with the specific content of the commentary.]

The clarification regarding the origin of these teachings is as follows: there are two causes for the existence of both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and duality (*dvaya*). Thus, nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Asaṅga petitioned Maitreya to expound the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Works such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* in its seventeen stages and the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra* were all spoken by Maitreya, as explained in detail in the extensive commentaries; however, there are slight differences, as noted on a separate sheet.

Second, regarding the explanation of the origin of the treatise (*śāstra*): the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states that there are two types of piṭakas: first, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka; second, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Within this, there are three categories: namely, the Sūtra, Abhidharma, and Vinaya. Thus, works such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā* are called the Sūtra-piṭaka within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka; the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and the *Abhidharmasūtra* are called the Abhidharma-piṭaka; and the *Vinayakṣudraka-sūtra* is called the third Piṭaka. However, the aforementioned sūtras exist only in their Sanskrit originals and consist of many verses; as they gradually fell into obscurity, the scrolls became small, or perhaps the translators here in this land were particularly abbreviated, which is why they have become increasingly concise.
In the *Abhidharma-sūtra*, there is a chapter titled "Compendium of the Mahāyāna," which was spoken by a Bodhisattva under the Buddha’s empowerment.

More than nine hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga compiled the essential meanings of various sūtras and composed the *Abhidharma-śāstra* in twenty-seven thousand verses.
Later, his disciple Buddhasimha—whose name means "Lion of Awakening"—composed a commentary of sixty-three thousand verses; these two versions were circulated separately from one another.

Later, there was a bodhisattva named Sthiramati who compiled these [works] into a single treatise; thus it is called the *Saṃgrahaṇī* (Compendium). It constitutes one branch among the ten branches of the *Yogācārabhūmi*, for works such as the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* each constitute a separate branch.
For example, three hundred years after Kātyāyanīputra composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, there subsequently appeared the "Six Feet" (*Ṣaṭpāda*) treatises and others.

Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, there are two parts: first, the elucidation of the Sūtra; second, the elucidation of the Śāstra.
Regarding the sūtras: since ancient times, there have been five translations of this *Prajñāpāramitā* in total; their respective dates are fully detailed in the *Xuanji*.

However, when the Tripiṭaka Master first arrived from the West at the beginning of the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he translated the śāstras first, with the *Abhidharmakośa* being the initial work.

In the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era, the Tripitaka Master accompanied the imperial entourage to Yuhua Palace. As the late Emperor’s health declined, he frequently performed meritorious deeds and translated treatises together with the Master. He ordained five men in succession and further inquired about their virtuous causes; the Master then instructed them to propagate and praise the teachings, whereupon [the Emperor] composed the preface to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, titled the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka."

At that time, the Prince also composed a preface to the *Xianyang lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Mahāyāna). He intended to permit the simultaneous translation of various sūtras and śāstras and to offer praises to the profound spirits; however, as he was already unwell, he did not have the leisure to compose extensively.
At that time, the Emperor asked Venerable Xuanzang,
"What further good deeds may be practiced? Xuanzang replied:
"You may take up the brush to compile the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Once the Emperor had granted his permission, Kumārajīva translated it;

that very night, at the third watch of the fifth period, the translation was completed. The Emperor requested to read it and immediately dispatched the relevant officials to transcribe ten thousand copies. Because it was not revised or compiled again, the phrasing and sentences became somewhat loose. Later, when he wished to retranslate it, there was no way to revise or adopt what had already been laid out previously.

When the Sanskrit manuscripts from successive dynasties were all entrusted to the Tripitaka Master, he collated various versions using the Sanskrit texts as his standard. These included the version translated by Kumārajīva, which was identical to the "Kunlun" manuscript, as well as the version translated by Paramārtha. However, the scriptural texts differed in their discrepancies; one could discern the authentic from the erroneous only by following the wording. While the titles varied, the Tripitaka Master alone titled it *Nengduan* (The Ability to Sever); this is the same title used for the previously translated version of Asaṅga’s commentary. What is the reason for this?
His intention is to explain that *vajra* has three meanings.
First, the meaning of "that which is to be destroyed. The root text of the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states: "the practice of right view and the practice of wrong view. The commentary explains:
although right and wrong views differ, they function identically; therefore, "practice" encompasses both types of views.
This is illustrated by the fact that although a vajra is a single entity, there is a distinction between its capacity and its object.
Even though it is called a "vajra," there are things capable of breaking it; thus, for example, the horns of a white sheep can indeed break a vajra.
Second, the meaning of "able to destroy": As Vasubandhu states, first, it is "subtle" because it is the cause of wisdom;
second, it is "firm" because it cannot be destroyed.

The commentary explains: Because the two types of wisdom—those arising from hearing and reflection—can suppress defilements, they gradually give rise to the wisdom of cultivation; thus, they are called "capable of crushing" and are termed the cause of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Second, "firm" refers to the wisdom of cultivation; since it is a concentrated mind that is truly capable of destroying obstacles, it is called "firm."
Alternatively, within the cultivation of wisdom, there is a distinction between the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), which serves to differentiate the subtle from the firm;
or, within the untainted, there are two further modes—the path of suppression and the path of abandonment—which both function.
However, the afflictive hindrances are subdued through both principle and phenomenon contemplations, because they are subdued by means of rejoicing in the higher realms and loathing the lower;
it should be understood that the cognitive hindrances are subdued solely through principle contemplation.

Furthermore, regarding the distinction between the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), as well as the division into "subtle" and "firm," that which is termed "abandonment" within the path of liberation at the stage of Buddhahood is designated as "abandonment" by virtue of its nature of abandonment and its category of abandonment among the three types of abandonment; it is not, however, the functional activity of abandonment nor the substantial essence of abandonment. This is because that which is not itself to be abandoned is not called "abandonment," and since its substance has already been abandoned rather than being currently undergoing abandonment, it is not termed the "agent of abandonment."
Third is the meaning of broadness and narrowness. The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states: "It is like a painted image of a vajra, which is wide at both ends and narrow at the waist.

The commentary explains: The stages prior to the ground (*bhūmi*) and the fruit of Buddhahood are metaphorically "broad," while the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) are metaphorically "narrow," because within each of those grounds, the cultivation of a single practice is taken as the primary focus;
alternatively, the stages from the seventh ground downward may be considered "broad," and all other cases should be understood accordingly based on their respective meanings.
It should be understood that if that which is destroyed is called "vajra," it is the vajra of prajñā;
if that which destroys and crushes is called "vajra," then the vajra is itself prajñā.
However, the Sūtra states that *prajñā* refers to wisdom within the causal stage;
*sarvajña* means "all-knowing," which is the wisdom within the resultant stage;
and *pratisaṃvid-jñāna* (or *pratisaṃkhyāna*) refers to the wisdom that severs delusions, which is precisely what is indicated here; therefore, it is said to be "capable of severing."
Regarding this treatise, there are currently three versions circulating in the land of Tang:
the first is said to have been composed by Vasubandhu, translated in either two or three fascicles.
Second, that composed by Asanga, consisting of either one or two fascicles.
Third, that composed by Vajrabodhi—namely, the man from Wu in the Southern Land—which is not an authentic holy teaching; this consists of either eleven or thirteen fascicles.
If one studies only that which exists and not emptiness, the mind of false conceptualization will grow ever more extensive;
if one studies only emptiness and not existence, true wisdom will have no cause and thus fail to arise.
One extinguishes false conceptualization at the gate of emptiness and gives rise to the true mind at the repository of existence; thus, emptiness and existence are like a pair of mirrors.
There are two kinds of teaching:
first, that which accords with capacities, such as the principles of the Four Noble Truths and the two kinds of emptiness.
Second, this refers to manifesting the principle as it truly is, by teaching such things as "signlessness" (*animitta*) and "reality-identity" (*tathatā*).

Regarding the Buddha’s single voice and so forth, the *Avataṃsaka* states that within a single word of the Tathāgata, he brings forth an ocean of boundless sūtras. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* clarifies only the inclusion [of all vehicles] to demonstrate the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), whereas the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda* provides a comprehensive basis for both their emergence and their inclusion.
However, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that if a person practices the five *pāramitās*, they do not equal one who receives, upholds, and hears the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Since "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) is a general designation for both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, the ox-cart is used as a metaphor for *bodhi*.
The Sūtra says: "I have fashioned these carts for you; therefore, you should each be given one with an impartial mind.
Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that practicing the six pāramitās does not equal holding this sūtra in one's hand.
He takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as his vehicle, as the characteristics thereof are fully revealed in that sūtra.
Thus have I heard.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Third, regarding the analysis of the main text: this sutra consists of three parts from beginning to end.
First, the introductory section;
second, the section on the request for extensive exposition, beginning with the words, "At that time, Subhūti rose from his seat"; [and third, the section on the actual exposition].
Following this, the section beginning with "After the Buddha had spoken this sutra" is the Part on Joyful Awakening and Practice.
Within the preceding [section], there are two parts:
first, the general causes and conditions; second, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, the specific causes and conditions.
The preceding section consists of five parts.
First, in order to inspire faith, the fact that [the teaching] has already been heard is generally indicated by saying, "Thus have I heard.
Second, because the speaker and the listener met together at a single time without distinction, it is generally stated as "at one time."
Third, every transformation [of the Buddha] must have a master; if the master is preeminent, the Dharma may be honored, and thus it is designated as "the Buddha.

Fourth, every transformation must have a location; one must rely upon a preeminent place to preach the sublime Dharma, and thus it is stated: "In the Kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park."

5. Clarifying the capacities of those for whom the teaching is intended: the phrase "accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people" refers, in actuality, to the assembly of bodhisattvas as spoken of by the Bhagavān, as well as the eight classes of beings as explained in the subsequent *Pariṇāmanā* section; however, because this [section] is abbreviated, only the śrāvakas are mentioned here.

The remaining text may be understood. Regarding the place called *Vasu*: it is pronounced *Hian-qing-hu-du* (顯輕呼度). The old transcription "Five India" (*Wu Tianzhu*) is erroneous. Now, as for the explanation of *Hian-du* (顯度): this is translated here as *Yuezhi* (月氏).
In these five kingdoms there are many sages and wise men; like the moon illuminating the darkness, they are able to dispel the scorching heat, and thus they were given this name.
Previous claims that they were the "Yuezhi" and so forth are all incorrect.

That which is called the kingdom of Śrāvastī is a corruption; it should be called Śrāvastīpura, which means "City of Abundant Virtue," because it abounds in extensive learning, abounds in objects of desire, and abounds in liberation.
The ruler of this city is King Pramāṇarāja, which in the Chinese language means "Victorious Army" (Shèngjūn); this is the name of the capital city of Central India.
The name of the country is Kośala; because it is distinguished from the Kośala located south of the Ganges River, it is identified by the name of its capital city.
As for that southern Kośala country, its capital has no distinct appellation and is therefore named after the country itself.
"Jeta’s Grove" refers to the grove belonging to Prince Jeta.
"Jeta" means "Victorious in Battle" in this language.
"Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park" refers to the fact that Sudatta purchased it from the Prince.
Now, in order to designate them together, both are mentioned here.
A detailed exposition of the dependent origination is as set forth in other commentaries.
[The Buddha] was accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The commentary states: This fifth section clarifies the capacity of the audience for whom the teaching is intended.
"With" (*saha*) refers to the Buddha’s common assembly; as Nāgārjuna explains, there are two meanings: first, being in the same place, namely the city of Abhyudaya;
second, being at the same time, because the speaking and listening reach their conclusion simultaneously.
Third, they share the same mind, because they together attain the single flavor of the Dharma;
fourth, they share the same view, because they equally realize the principle of liberation;
fifth, they share the same precepts, because each possesses the prātimokṣa vows.
Sixth, they share the same liberation, because the three vehicles sit together upon the bed of liberation.
Possessing such meanings, it is collectively termed "giving" (*yǔ*).
As for "Great" (*dà*), there are five meanings: first, greatness of name, because he is known by the great assembly and great beings; [and so forth].
Second, greatness of stage: they all abide in the fruits of sainthood and are therefore not in the stage of ordinary beings;
third, greatness of merit: either their outflows are exhausted, as they have realized wisdom and eliminated [afflictions];
fourth, greatness of practice: they seek great enlightenment and cultivate vast activities.
Fifth, because his retinue is great, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
Nāgārjuna’s commentary states: "For example, where there are seven treasures, gold is the greatest;
even in a place where there are no fine things, an iron hoe is the greatest."
Thus, when the Three Jewels exist, the Buddha is the greatest;
even until the final age, the monk who has broken the precepts becomes the greatest.
Therefore, a sutra says: "Though a *campaka* flower may be withered, it still surpasses all other flowers when they are fresh and pure."
Because even bhikṣus who break the precepts and engage in evil conduct are superior to those outside the path (tīrthika) who uphold the precepts.
The term "great" used here is intended provisionally in contrast to those still in training (śaikṣa).
As for the term "bhikṣu," it has five meanings.
First, the Frightener of Māras: because the four Māras are terrified when one first resolves to leave the household life.
Second, the Mendicant: because one sustains oneself by begging, thereby balancing the needs of oneself and others.
Third, pure livelihood (*ājīva-śuddhi*): because one abandons the five types of wrong livelihood and rectifies the three karmas of body, speech, and mind. The five types of wrong livelihood are:

first, manifesting wonders for the sake of gain and honor, such as sitting in meditation while counting prayer beads; second, speaking of one’s own virtues for the sake of gain and honor; [third, disparaging others for the sake of gain and honor;
fourth, hinting at what one possesses for the sake of gain and honor; fifth, using flattery for the sake of gain and honor.]
Third, to gain profit and offerings, one divines signs of good and ill fortune;
fourth, to gain profit and offerings, one raises one's voice and displays an air of authority;
fifth, to obtain profit and offerings, one speaks of past gains to move the hearts of others.
Fourth, the nature of upholding the precepts, because their dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) is never deficient.
Fifth, the destruction of evil: by cultivating the path, one attains the fruit and severs the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The term *saṃgha* is translated as "assembly" (*zhòng*), because both the realization of principle and the performance of Dharma-affairs are in harmony.
Regarding the "one thousand two hundred and fifty persons": when the Buddha first attained enlightenment, during the first period, he converted the five men, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya;
during the second period, he converted Yaśas and others, numbering fifty people;
and during the third period, he converted Śāriputra and others, numbering one hundred people.
In the fourth period, he converted one hundred people, including Maudgalyāyana;
in the fifth period, he converted five hundred people, including Uruvilvākāśyapa;
and in the sixth period, he converted two hundred and ninety-five people, including Gayākāśyapa.
In the seventh period, he delivered two hundred people, including Nadī-Kāśyapa and others.
Thus, there were one thousand two hundred and fifty people in total; this refers to his constant retinue.
Accordingly, there are also assemblies of bhikṣuṇīs and so forth below, but they are omitted here for the sake of brevity.
However, the *Āgama Sūtras* are taught solely for those who have set out to seek the Śrāvaka Vehicle;

the teaching of Prajñā-emptiness is taught solely for those who have set out to seek the Mahāyāna. Therefore, it is said below that [this teaching] is for the sake of those of the Mahāyāna, and for the sake of those of the Supreme Vehicle.

The *Nirvāṇa*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Saṃdhinirmocana*, and other such sutras are taught in common for those who aspire to all vehicles; that is to say, they teach that conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are "existent," while the self and what belongs to the self are taught to be "empty."

Therefore, those currently listed as the assembly of śrāvakas are included here precisely for the purpose of inciting them to set out and seek the Mahāyāna; since the bodhisattvas have already set out, they are not explicitly designated here.
The preceding section concludes the clarification of the general causes and conditions.
At that time, at the hour of eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location.
Having finished eating, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat, and sat down.
The commentary states: Second, the clarification of the specific causes and conditions.
This section contains ten parts:

1. Clarifying the principal teacher of the transformation refers to "the World-Honored One"; 2. Distinguishing the time of the transformation refers to "at mealtime"; 3. Manifesting the robes refers to "having put on his robes"; 4. Revealing the holding of the vessel refers to "carrying his almsbowl"; 5. Describing the field of conversion refers to "entering the great city of Śrāvastī"; 6. Clarifying the seeking of food refers to "begging for alms"; 7. Distinguishing the universal impartiality refers to "having begged in order throughout that city"; 8. Manifesting the gathering of those to be transformed refers to "returning to his original place"; 9. Revealing the washing of the feet refers to "having finished eating, having put away his robes and bowl, and having washed his feet"; 10. Describing the peaceful abiding refers to "spreading out a seat and sitting down."
Regarding the term "World-Honored One" (Bhagavān), it refers to one who possesses six qualities and has destroyed the four māras.

The four māras are well known; as for the six qualities, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* explains them as follows: first, the sense of sovereignty, because he is forever unbound by any afflictions (*kleśa*);
second, the sense of blazing intensity, because he has been refined and tempered by the fiercely burning fire of wisdom.
Third, the meaning of majesty and dignity, because he is adorned with all the primary and secondary marks;
fourth, the meaning of renown, because there is nothing among all his supreme virtues that is not fully known;
fifth, the meaning of auspiciousness, because all those in the world who approach him to offer worship unanimously praise him.

Sixth, the meaning of reverence: because one possesses all virtues and constantly applies skillful means to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings without ever becoming weary or negligent.
The term "at the time of eating" refers to the time of the midday meal.

Each of the following items has its own symbolic significance; thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states that the Buddha told Ānanda: "Whatever postures and movements all Buddhas undertake are none other than Buddha-activities."
Why is it now said that it is "mealtime"?

This indicates that the sutra was preached after the meal had been finished; at that moment, the sun was precisely at its zenith. This signifies that the Mahāyāna principle of signlessness (*animitta*) expounded therein abandons the dualistic attachments to the extremes of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and existence (*bhāva*). Therefore, "mealtime" refers specifically to the particular time when this sutra was preached.

This indicates that when one wishes to expound the teaching of signlessness, one first contemplates the principle of signlessness; it is like wishing to expound the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, where one first enters the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meanings and contemplates the principle of the station of immeasurable meanings.

The Buddha takes wisdom as his life and the signless (*animitta*) as his sustenance. Desiring to expound the teaching of the signless, he first contemplates the subtle principle of the signless through wisdom, and only thereafter does he preach it; therefore, it is called "the time of eating."

Regarding "putting on the robes," there are three types of robes: the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsaka*. Among these, the first robe is worn when entering royal cities or villages; the second is worn when addressing the assembly to preach the Dharma; and the third is understood accordingly.
Now, as one wishes to enter a city, one puts on the initial garment;

likewise, within the Dharma there are also three robes. The first is diligence, which is also called armor (*kavaca*); this refers to being able to exert oneself in proclaiming matters of benefit and happiness, and not avoiding cold, heat, and other such conditions, just like wearing a garment.

2. The gentle robe of patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti-vastra*): This means that by means of patience one wards off external [aggressors], so that hostile harms cannot invade; it is like wearing a garment, whereby cold and heat do not touch the body.

Third, "the superior garment of shame and remorse" (hrī-apatrāpya): because it consists of honoring and respecting the noble and good while rejecting the violent and evil, with a sense of shame as its characteristic, it is like a robe.
Now, this represents the Buddha’s diligent proclamation of the wondrous Dharma of signlessness; therefore, it is said that he "wears the robes."

Regarding "carrying the almsbowl": it is a vessel of appropriate measure. First, it should correspond to the amount one's own food requires; second, it should correspond to the amount of what is offered by others from outside. Because it is neither too large nor too small, it is called "of appropriate measure."
To signify that the Buddha’s non-conceptual wisdom internally realizes the principle— just as a bowl receives food—
and that the mind gives rise to wisdom, it is further called "holding.
As for "entering the great city of Śrāvastī," it signifies the desire to enter the great city of the True Dharma to partake of the food of signlessness.
Alternatively, the True Dharma is like a city; thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* speaks of "going to protect the city of the Dharma," for the Bodhisattva is like the guardian of the city.

Alternatively, the True Dharma is like the people within the city and the Bodhisattva is like the city itself; this is the reading where "protecting the city of the Dharma" is pronounced with level tones.
Alternatively, it refers to entering the great city of the Dharma-realm and drinking the flavor of signlessness (*animitta*); to signify this, it says "entering the great city of Śrāvastī."
"Begging for food" (piṇḍapāta) correctly symbolizes the internal realization of the signless principle through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

"Begging in sequence" (sāvadāna-piṇḍapāta) means going from one alley to another and from one house to another, and so forth, to manifest that each and every phenomenon is universally realized as reaching the signless principle.

"Returning to his original place" signifies that in order to expound the teaching of signlessness, he must once again give rise to subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) to extensively propagate it for others.
"Washing his feet" reveals that while external impurities are removed by washing the feet, internal defilements are naturally extinguished upon hearing the Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "spreading the seat and sitting," it means that because the Blessed One wished to manifest the supreme nature of the Dharma he was about to teach, he personally spread his own seat; as if beholding a position of honor, he did not have anyone else prepare the seating materials.

Regarding the phrase "and sat," the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* explains that this demonstrates that only those who are utterly tranquil are able to realize and teach the Dharma; thus, the depiction of the Blessed One with body erect and mindfulness established serves to indicate that he internally realizes the truth and externally teaches the signless Dharma.

The *Vajracchedikā* states, "abiding with the back turned and the face turned toward [the object]. Here, "back" (*pṛṣṭha*) signifies remoteness, while "face" (*mukha*) signifies the sense of looking toward. This means that one contemplates the principle through wisdom, just as a mirror reflects a face.
What is called "turning one's back" means turning one's back on birth and death;
"facing toward" means facing toward nirvana.
Turning one's back means abandoning afflictions.
The "face" signifies the realization of ultimate truth;
the "back" signifies the departure from both existence and emptiness;
the "face" signifies abiding in the Middle Way.
It should be understood in this way.
Alternatively, what is called "mindfulness facing [the object]" has the meaning of "gazing"; that is to say, because one penetrates the principle through wisdom, it is like gazing upon a face.

At that time, the Elder Subhūti, being among the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

The commentary states: This is the second of the major sections, the "Request for Explanation. Within the "Section on the Actual Exposition," according to Vasubandhu’s structural analysis, there are two parts. Specifically, from this point up to "the retribution is also inconceivable" constitutes the first cycle of exposition; next, from "At that time, Subhūti" down to "how should one abide," and continuing until "one should contemplate in this manner," constitutes the second cycle of exposition.

This refers to the three questions posed during the first cycle: how one who has not yet generated the resolve can generate it, up to how one who is already engaged in practice can eliminate obstacles.

As for what was said during the second cycle: if a bodhisattva were to give rise to such thoughts regarding their own threefold practice as "I am able to generate the resolve," up to "I am able to eliminate obstacles," [the Buddha taught] the second cycle in order to eliminate such overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
This means that during the first cycle of teaching, the Dharma was explained to clarify how those who have not yet resolved their minds are instructed to do so;
as for the second cycle of teaching, it was spoken for those who have already resolved their minds, saying "I am able to resolve my mind," and thus [the Buddha] taught them accordingly.

Alternatively, there are two distinct explanations for the two cycles of "cultivation" and "severing hindrances. The older commentary states that the first cycle is for generating this goodness, while the second cycle is for severing hindrances; these hindrances refer specifically to the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Thus, the subsequent treatise says: "Cultivating within the internal mind, one maintains the notion of being a bodhisattva"—this is precisely what obstructs the path of non-abiding.

This means that because a Bodhisattva does not abide within the path, but rather realizes it by means of non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna) through inwardly merging with ultimate truth, they do not give rise to a mind of "I" or "self.

Furthermore, it is explained that two cycles of teaching were given for the sake of the two types of capacities—sharp and dull—and the two groups of practitioners—those at the beginning and those at the end of the path.
Within the first cycle, there are two parts: from "In this way one should subdue [the mind]" down to "abide as instructed" constitutes the main body of the teaching;

from "Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? onwards clarifies the severing of doubts—specifically, the *prajñā* that serves as the path capable of severing, and that which is to be severed, namely the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*).

The preceding section consists of four parts: first, Subhūti’s reverent praise and request; second, the Tathāgata’s commendation, seal of approval, and permission to speak; third, his respectful assent and desire to hear; and fourth, the detailed answers given according to the questions.
Within the preceding section there are three parts:
first, the clarification of reverent devotion; second, the clarification of praise; and third, the formal presentation of the request. This is the first of those sections.

Now, once the Bodhisattva Asaṅga has explained the establishment of the seven categories of meaning, this Prajñāpāramitā is thereby established—namely, the non-interruption of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and so forth.
Regarding these seven [points], the first three categorize this sutra as a whole, consisting of three sections;
the latter four reveal the meanings contained within this sutra and do not constitute a separate textual analysis.
Regarding the three-part text:
first, Subhūti’s praise is termed the non-interruption of the lineage;
second, Subhūti’s request for instruction is termed the manifestation of the aspect of arousal, because it initiates the inquiry into the aspects of practice.

Third, the Tathāgata’s sealed response concludes with the instruction, "One should contemplate in this manner," which is called the locus where practice abides. This means that by relying on the meaning of this specific section as taught by the Buddha to carry out one's practice, it constitutes the locus where practice abides.

Fourth, regarding the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), there is no separate textual passage; rather, within the very places where one dwells while practicing, there exist both the antidote and that which is to be countered.

Thus, the treatise states: "When one practices such corresponding modes of conduct while dwelling in those various stations, it should be known that there are two kinds of antidotes: namely, wrong practice and right practice accompanied by views. Herein, "view" refers to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).

Within the first stage (bhūmi), if it is said that a bodhisattva should generate such a thought as "all sentient beings," this is the antidote to wrong practice; for to generate such a thought is itself a wrong practice for a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, if it is said, "If a bodhisattva has the notion of a sentient being," and so forth, this is the antidote to the common view regarding correct practice; this conceptual grasping by the bodhisattva must also be abandoned, namely, the thought, "I should deliver sentient beings."

In the second dwelling, if it is said that "one should practice giving," this is an antidote to wrong practice; it does not mean that the absence of giving constitutes a wrong practice for a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, if it is said that "one dwells in things" and so forth, this is an antidote to the correct practice of common views; such conceptual grasping by a bodhisattva must also be abandoned, namely, the notion that one "should practice giving."
Within this context, there are the remedies and the objects to be remedied, which should be explained accordingly.
Fifth, "non-loss" means not losing the right path; this excludes the attachments to increase and decrease.
This means that because one clings to the existence of persons and phenomena within the sphere where conditioned activities abide, it is called "clinging to increase";
because one denies the existence of the sublime Dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*), it is called "clinging to decrease.
If one acts in this way, one loses the right path; now, by negating these two types of clinging, it is said that "one does not lose [the path]."

Therefore, the Treatise states: "In this regard, if it is said, 'The nature of merit that the Tathāgata speaks of is itself not a nature of merit,' this negates the extreme of superimposition (*samāropa*), because there is no self-nature (*svabhāva*) in the conceptualization of that mass of merit.

If it is further said, 'Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of the Tathāgata’s mass of merit,' this negates the extreme of denial (*apavāda*), because although it does not possess a self-nature as it exists in words, there is nevertheless a referent that can be spoken of, since the Tathāgata speaks of a mass of merit. Even up to the statement, "What is called the Buddha-dharma is itself not the Buddha-dharma," all such instances should be explained accordingly; this is termed "not losing [the meaning]."
Sixth, regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three types:

first, the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita-bhūmi*), which refers to the position of cultivation for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), beginning from the proclamation up to "this is called all dharmas";
second, the stage of the pure mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*), which refers to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), beginning from "for example, as when a person's body grows large."
Third, the Stage of the Buddha (*buddhabhūmi*), which extends from the passage, "If a bodhisattva were to say, 'I shall adorn the buddha-fields,'" up to the end of the sutra.
Seventh, regarding the establishment of the title: this refers to the explanation of the name *Prajñāpāramitā* (The Perfection of Wisdom), by means of which [the meaning] may be understood.

However, as for the *Vajrasena-śāstra* existing in the southern regions, which divides this treatise into twelve sections, this is merely a speculative fabrication based on the mundane sentiments of those here; it is not to be relied upon.

Regarding the phrase "At that time, the Elder": in the Western regions, those of advanced age are designated as "Elders" (*sthavira*). However, if one is young yet possesses virtue, they may still bear the title of "Great Virtue" (*bhadanta*); this is not a universal rule restricted to a specific region.

"Subhūti" is an erroneous transcription; it should be "Subhūti," which means "Good Manifestation. He was foremost among the disciples of the World-Honored One in understanding emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This means that he was able to manifest his birth during the era of a Buddha; or, he was well able to manifest a thorough realization of the meaning of emptiness; or, when he first appeared at birth, his chamber was empty and still, and an interpreter of signs named him "Good Manifestation."

"Manifest" (*Abhirati*) means "to emerge. At the time of his birth, the entire chamber was empty and still; this signified that as he grew up, he would skillfully understand the meaning of emptiness. Therefore, he is named "Good Manifestation" (*Subhūti*).

Regarding the new translation of the *Prajñāpāramitā* (the *Nengduan*), which names him "Venerable Subhūti": there are two kinds of life. First is supramundane life, which refers to wisdom; second is mundane life, which refers to the continuity that maintains the succession of form and mind.
If one were to designate him solely as "Wisdom-Life" (*prajñājīvita*), he would not encompass the mundane;
if one were to speak only of "Life" (*āyuṣ*), it would not apply to the supramundane. To manifest that he possesses both, he is called "Possessing Life" (*āyuṣmat*).
Thus, Subhūti has two aspects: first, he has attained the supramundane life of wisdom; second, he has attained a long life within the world; for these reasons, he is also called "Elder" (sthavira).
"Rising from his seat" signifies the relinquishing of the non-authentic vehicles of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and the proceeding toward the ultimate goal of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
"Baring the right shoulder" displays the aspect of reverence, for the right side is considered auspicious; it signifies that Prajñāpāramitā bestows blessings and prosperity upon the multitude.

"Placing the right knee on the ground" signifies the subduing of the faults of birth and death; that is to say, because one has committed various transgressions with the right hand and foot since beginningless time, this gesture demonstrates that the Dharma is capable of subduing the suffering of birth and death.
"Joining the palms" signifies that the mind of the listener is in harmonious union with the Dharma.
"Reverence" signifies that the Dharma is worthy of honor.
The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* states that Subhūti’s question arises from six causes and conditions.

First, to sever doubt: this means that since beginningless time, sentient beings have possessed ignorance within themselves; obscured by the delusions of afflictions, they give rise to doubts—namely, doubts regarding the Four Truths or the Triple Gem—and are thus unable to engender faith. When he poses his question, all such doubts are completely severed.

Second, "for the sake of giving rise to faith and understanding" means that although one may possess faith, if one does not know upon which sūtras and dharmas to base that faith and understanding, one asks questions so as to cause the arising of faith and understanding regarding the Prajñāpāramitā.

Third, for the sake of those entering the profound: this means that although one may have developed faith and understanding regarding Prajñā, one has not yet been able to advance in understanding its profound meaning; therefore, one asks questions so as to bring about the understanding of that profound meaning.

Fourth, regarding "for the sake of non-retrogression": this means that although one has attained understanding of the profound, one might occasionally regress due to conditions such as mosquitoes, gadflies, quarrels, or fatigue; however, by asking questions, one ensures there is never any retrogression.

Fifth, "for the sake of generating joy" means that sentient beings have long cultivated the cycle of birth and death, constantly harboring immeasurable and manifold sorrows and sufferings; by asking a single question, these sorrows and sufferings are forever eliminated, and thus joy is produced.

Sixth, regarding "for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma": this means that if such Prajñā were not taught, or if the various aspects of the True Dharma were to quickly vanish and perish due to a lack of anyone to uphold them, then by posing this question, one shall cause the True Dharma to endure forever.
“Rare indeed, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains all bodhisattvas, and skillfully entrusts all bodhisattvas.
The commentary states: according to Vasubandhu’s topical outline, there are two sections within the first cycle.
I. The section on requesting the teaching according to the specific school;
II. The section on extensively refuting the doubts of the assembly, beginning from "It can be [known] by means of bodily marks.
Within the first [section], there are four parts:
I. Reverent Praise and Entreaty; II. Praising the Granting of Permission and Presenting [the Request]; III. Respectful Acceptance and the Hope to Hear; IV. Answering Each Question in Turn.
Regarding the first [section], there are four parts: first, manifesting the location, namely, within the great assembly;
second, manifesting reverent devotion; [and so forth].
Third, the praise; fourth, the formal request.
The preceding two sections are concluded; this is the third section, the praise.
To say, "It is rare, World-Honored One," means that within the *kalpa* of abiding (*vivartakalpa*), Buddhas appear only at certain times and in certain places.

For instance, among the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, four have already appeared in the world; that is to say, during the first five *kalpas* of this *kalpa* of abiding, no Buddha appeared in the world.
In the sixth *kalpa*, when the human lifespan was forty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appeared in the world.
In the seventh kalpa, when the human lifespan was thirty thousand years, Kanakamuni Buddha appeared in the world;
in the eighth kalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world;
and in the ninth kalpa, when the human lifespan was one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appeared.
In the tenth kalpa, during the initial phase of the decreasing aeon when the human lifespan was eighty thousand years, Maitreya Buddha appeared;
by the fifteenth kalpa, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas appeared together in a single kalpa;
and in the subsequent abiding kalpa, there was the Buddha Loushi (Ruci) who appeared alone during that entire abiding kalpa.
From this point onward, after further passing twelve great kalpas, the first Buddha of the Star宿 Kalpa, Sūryaprabha (Sunlight), will appear;
from that time onward, after another three hundred kalpas have passed, other Buddhas will appear in the world.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is remote and difficult to encounter," and so forth.

Regarding "skillfully protecting and mindful of [them]," Vasubandhu states: "Bestowing [benefits] upon their persons and practicing together with them. First, bestowing [benefits] upon their persons; second, bestowing [benefits] upon those who practice the same pure conduct (*brahmacārin*).

This refers to bodhisattvas who have already awakened the aspiration for enlightenment and encountered various Buddhas; when their faculties have matured, the Tathāgata immediately protects and mindfully attends to them, bestowing all empowerments upon their persons so that they may attain self-benefit and increase wholesome dharmas.

Second, the addition of practicing together (*sahācaryā*), which means that when a bodhisattva has fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*), they cause them to turn toward teaching others, thereby augmenting their altruism.

"Well-entrusted" refers to those bodhisattvas whose faculties (*indriya*) are not yet mature; although they have already generated the resolve [for awakening], their spiritual capacity is not yet ripened. This is of two kinds:
first, those who have never previously possessed merit (*guṇa*).
Second, although these two types of individuals may have previously possessed merit, they have already fallen away from it.

Therefore, they are entrusted to Bodhisattvas whose faculties are matured, who are charged with instructing them: to cause those who have not yet attained [the goal] to attain it, and to cause those who have already attained but then regressed to advance further in their practice; thus, this is called "entrustment" (*parindanā*).

Furthermore, regarding "causing those who have attained non-retrogression not to abandon the Mahāyāna": previously, those whose faculties were not yet mature were entrusted to those whose faculties were already mature; now, the World-Honored One entrusts the Dharma to those whose faculties are not yet mature, causing them not to abandon the Mahāyāna and desiring that they achieve further progress within it—this is termed "entrustment" (*parindanā*).

Master Shiyi says that, according to the treatise, there are two kinds of entrustment: first, among bodhisattvas, there are those who have regressed and those who have not; simply causing them not to abandon the Mahāyāna and causing them to advance further is what is meant by "entrustment."

However, Asaṅga’s interpretation differs slightly from this; his intention is stated as follows: when the Tathāgata first attained enlightenment, there were bodhisattvas who had previously accumulated roots of merit in the past and whose faculties were already matured. For them, the Buddha immediately taught the locus where those practices abide. Within that locus, he taught that the Noble Path is the antidote and conceptual discrimination is that which is to be countered.

Furthermore, it is said that by severing the two attachments to increase and decrease, one does not lose the right path—whether in the cultivation of ordinary beings, the cultivation of bodhisattvas, or the stage of Buddhahood.
Moreover, it is said that this is called "skillfully protecting and mindful care" because it establishes the name of *prajñā*.

Those who are "well-entrusted" are bodhisattvas whose faculties are not yet mature and who have not yet been able to resolve their minds toward practice; therefore, as the Tathāgata approaches nirvāṇa, he entrusts them and takes them into his care, commanding them to teach according to these five meanings and likewise causing them to bring the Buddha-dharma to maturity.
Those who have already been taken into care are those bodhisattvas whose faculties have matured. Furthermore, there are six aspects of protective mindfulness (*anurakṣaṇā*):

first, regarding time, it means that the Tathāgata is able to provide protective mindfulness for both the present and the future. This refers to the time when he causes them to dwell in peace and happiness in the present, thereby preventing them from committing evil that would bring about evil results in the future; this is called "benefit" (*hitāya*). It is not like a compassionate mother who, while seeking to give her child pleasure in the present, might instead cause him to commit evil.
Second is differentiation, meaning that one is well able to discern the differences in capacities and preach accordingly; thus it is called "skillfully protecting and mindful of.
Third is loftiness, meaning that by means of *prajñā*, one gathers and benefits sentient beings, and there is nothing superior to this.
Fourth, regarding "firmness": while worldly things may be subject to destruction, this prajñā is ultimately and absolutely firm.
Fifth, regarding "universality": it means that it can universally encompass and benefit both oneself and others; thus, it is not like the Two Vehicles, which seek only self-benefit.

Sixth, regarding "distinctive characteristics" (*vilakṣaṇa*): this refers to the fact that within the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*), there are various distinctions among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in their state of cultivation; according to these differences, the teaching is given by means of distinct and diverse methods.
There are also six kinds of "skillful entrustment.
First, the "place of entry" (praveśa): that to which one turns for refuge is called the place of entry; "place" here refers to a secure dwelling.

This refers to the Buddha’s entrustment to those whose faculties are not yet mature, saying, "After my parinirvāṇa, you shall take refuge in other bodhisattvas and buddhas," and so forth; therefore, one takes various spiritual friends as the objects of refuge.

Second, regarding those who attain it through the nature of things (*dharmatā*): this refers to those whose faculties have already matured, who are naturally able to provide benefit and assistance to others, just as a mother does for her child.
Third, "transmitting the teaching" means causing the profound Dharma of Prajñā to be proclaimed, so that the transmission of the lamp may be inherited without interruption.
Fourth, "not losing" refers to the point of entry; because there is a place to which one can take refuge, one does not lose the True Dharma or the Right Path.
Fifth, compassion means that, by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), because one possesses compassion, one is able to benefit others through that same natural principle.
Sixth, reverence means transmission; for it is by revering *prajñā* that one is able to pass on the teaching from one to another.
“World-Honored One!
How should a son or daughter of good family who has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide?
How should they subdue their mind?”
The commentary states: This third section is the formal request for instruction.
The phrase "good sons" (*kulaputra*) and so forth refers specifically to the *upāsakas* and others.
If one does not receive the Prātimokṣa precepts, one cannot draw near to or serve [the teacher]; therefore, it is not called "wholesome.
"To bring forth" (utpāda) means to give birth to or to arise.
"Anuttara" means "unsurpassed" (wu shang); "saṃ" means "correct" (zheng);
"yak" means "equal" (děng).
"Three" (tri) is also called "correct" (samyak); "bodhi" is termed "awakening" (jñāna).

It should be expressed as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* or simply *saṃbodhi*. This means that the first term is the general name; the second distinguishes it from the false awakening of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); the third distinguishes it from the partial awakening of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*); and the fourth distinguishes it from the incomplete awakening of bodhisattvas. Because it denotes perfection, it is thus named *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
That which is called this "essence" is precisely the Dharma-body; thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata is the Dharma-body, and the Dharma-body is the realm of nirvāṇa."
Regarding the term "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*): it is called "arousing" because one proceeds toward *prajñā*.
As for the question "How does one abide?", it asks by abiding in what state of mind does one accomplish this arousal?
That is to say, in what state does one abide so as to bring forth [the resolve]?
"How does the world practice?"—once the resolve has been generated, how does one practice?
Regarding the question, "How does one subdue the mind?"—once one has already engaged in practice, how are the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) to be eliminated?
Regarding the question, "How does one abide?"—this refers to the profound mindfulness directed toward the minds of sentient beings.
"What is meant by 'how to practice'? refers to seeking the bodhicitta.
"What is meant by 'how to subdue'? refers to the mind of weary detachment from the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, "cutting off all evils" refers to "how to subdue the mind";
"cultivating all virtues" refers to "how to practice";
and "delivering all sentient beings" refers to "how to abide."

Furthermore, the *saṃvara-śīla* (vows of restraint), the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (vows of gathering virtuous dharmas), and the *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (vows of benefiting sentient beings) are also to be assigned accordingly.
The above explanations are all based on the intention of Vasubandhu; according to Asaṅga, they differ from the above.
Regarding what he said, "one should abide," this refers to desire (*chanda*) and aspiration (*praṇidhāna*). "Desire" means correct seeking; that is, it means seeking the Buddha correctly.
"Aspiration" means that which is sought; it refers to forming mental reflections, meaning one generates correct aspirations such as severing all evil and so forth.
"Should practice" means being in union with *samāpatti*; *samāpatti* refers to non-conceptual *samādhi*.
This means that, in order to counteract conceptualization, one gives rise to non-conceptual *samādhi* and brings forth non-conceptual wisdom.

This means that because of the presence of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), the notions of "is" and "is not" arise; because these notions arise, afflictions (*kleśa*) emerge; because afflictions emerge, one creates unwholesome karma; and because unwholesome karma is created, one revolves in birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Now, in order to sever these, one gives rise to non-conceptual practice (*nirvikalpa-caryā*).
"Discrimination" refers to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
"That which should be subdued" means the time for subduing distraction.
Regarding "the time for subduing distraction," it refers to when the mind of *samāpatti* becomes distracted; one must restrain it and cause it to return to abiding.
This means that if one subdues the discriminating mind so as not to allow it to become distracted, it is called "subjugation";
because one correctly gives rise to non-discriminative samāpatti, it is called "cultivation."
Question:

"For what reason is it not said that 'if a son of good family and others [wish to] abide in the enlightenment of the three vehicles, how should they abide,' etc., but instead is it spoken of only in relation to the Mahāyāna?"
As the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "Those who bear the four heavy burdens include both those with lineage and those without lineage, all of whom are to be benefited.

Therefore, the answer is given: "The commentary explains that this refers to the meaning of 'unattainability. That is to say, since Subhūti is a śrāvaka, if one were to ask whether the dwelling and practice of the Mahāyāna are unattainable for him, it would not be a difficult matter; however, as for asking about the dwelling and practice of the two vehicles [śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha], it is not a difficult task for him. Thus, the World-Honored One did not exclaim 'Excellent' [in response]."
Furthermore, because he asked skillfully regarding the distinctions among the three types of enlightenment, he inquired specifically about those who set out on the Bodhisattva vehicle.
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!”
Subhūti! As you have said, the Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas; listen now with close attention!
I shall now explain for you, son of good family, how a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide and how they should subdue their mind.
The commentary states: This is the second section, the Praise, Confirmation, and Declaration;
within it, there are three parts: first, the praise; second, the confirmation; and third, the declaration.
"Exclamation" (tàn) means "well done. This implies that if Subhūti had said something merely reasonable, the Buddha would have simply confirmed it, rather than praising it repeatedly;
however, because his question was both extremely profound and vast, the Buddha praised him repeatedly, saying, "Well done! (sādhu).
"Seal" (mudrā) means to seal or confirm those words;
"granting permission to speak" refers to the intention to proclaim them.
"Truthfully" (satya) means to examine closely; it causes one to listen and receive with careful scrutiny, hence the term "listen truthfully" (satyaṃ śṛṇu).

Therefore, the Sūtra says: "To those who listen with focused gaze as if they were hungry or thirsty, whose single mind enters into the meaning of the words, who leap for joy upon hearing the Dharma with hearts of both sorrow and delight—it is to such persons that one should preach."
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We wish and desire to hear it.
The commentary states: This is the third instance of respectfully assenting and expressing a desire to hear.
"Only" (唯) is a term of respect.
"So it is" (然) means that the matter may indeed be so.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way: regarding all categories of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether with form or without form;
whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception.”
The commentary states: This is the fourth section, providing specific answers to individual questions. Within it, first is the answer to the question "How does one dwell?";
next, from "Furthermore" onwards, is the answer to the question "How does one practice?";
and finally, "Subhūti!"... [text continues].
"From 'A bodhisattva should act thus' onwards, the answer concerns subduing.

Within the first [section] there are four parts: first, clarifying the vast mind; second, clarifying the foremost mind; third, clarifying the constant mind; and fourth, clarifying the non-perverted mind. This is the first."
The preceding follows the topical outline of Vasubandhu.

According to Asaṅga, if one speaks in terms of the distinctions within the third section—“the places where that practice is established”—there are eighteen; yet if categorized by way of the stages (*bhūmi*), there are three. That is to say: the first sixteen constitute the practices of ordinary beings during the two stages of the equipment (*saṃbhāra*) and application (*prayoga*) prior to the [first] stage, namely the Stage of Faithful Practice (*śraddhācaryā-bhūmi*);
the seventeenth, the Path of Realization (*adhigama-mārga*), is the practice of the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, namely the Stage of Pure Mind (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
The eighteenth is the Stage of Seeking the Supreme, which is the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*).

This refers to the section beginning with "I have already adorned the Buddha-lands. If categorized by way of dwelling places (*vihāra*), there are six; namely: first, the dwelling place of inclusion; second, the dwelling place of the purification of the perfections (*pāramitā-viśuddhi-vihāra*), and so forth. Among these, the first two dwelling places correspond to the first two of the eighteen stages.
Third, the dwelling place of desire refers to two among the eighteen, namely, the desire to attain the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Fourth, the dwelling place free from obstacles refers to the remaining twelve dwellings.
Fifth, the dwelling place of the pure mind refers to the seventeenth stage, the realization of the Way.
Sixth, the ultimate dwelling place refers to the eighteenth stage, the supreme seeking of the Buddha-ground.

Although there are eight dwelling places in total, the latter two are not separate from the former six; because they are common to all dwelling places, when speaking of dwelling places in general, there are only six kinds.

That is to say, for instance, within the first two dwelling places, there are both the vast and the profound types of dwelling places, as fully revealed in the treatise; other cases should be understood accordingly.

Among the six stages of abiding, the first four constitute the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita-bhūmi*); therein, the first two belong to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), and the latter two to the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
However, according to the intention of Asaṅga, which differs from Vasubandhu’s treatise, each of the eighteen distinctions provides answers to the three preceding questions.
Therefore, the treatise states: when the sūtra says that a bodhisattva should give rise to such a mind, it reveals the aspiration and vow within the context of how a bodhisattva should abide.

When it says that if a bodhisattva were to transform into the perception of sentient beings, they would not be a bodhisattva, this demonstrates the time of the samāpatti corresponding to such practice.

If a bodhisattva gives rise to the notion of a sentient being, the notion of a person, or the notion of a life-span, they are not called a bodhisattva; this demonstrates that one should thus subdue the mind when it is distracted during the process of concentration.

Regarding this, Vasubandhu answers the three questions by combining the first two of the eighteen distinctions, whereas Asaṅga answers each of the three questions individually; one should consult the treatise to understand this distinction.
Regarding the response to the question "How does one abide?": it refers to how one settles the mind so as to bring about its arousal.

This means that practitioners who wish to realize bodhi and accomplish great benefit and happiness must first arouse the mind of great enlightenment (*mahābodhicitta*) before they can initiate correct practice. Therefore, a sutra states: "Just as when the first knot of a bamboo is split, the remaining knots can be quickly split; so too, when the obstacles are first removed upon seeing the path, the remaining obstacles can be quickly removed."
If one generates the bodhicitta, all merits will naturally become perfected.

Therefore, regarding the generation of the bodhicitta, the sutras state that it is like the first drop in the great ocean, which serves as the basis for all treasures; the initial generation of the mind is likewise so, for the wholesome dharmas of the five vehicles all arise from this.

Furthermore, just as the initial arising of the world serves as the cause for supporting all sentient beings, so too does this mind serve as the basis for supporting the immeasurable varieties within the five destinies.

Furthermore, just as the realm of space contains and accommodates all things, so too is the great bodhicitta: because it universally feels weary of and detached from all conditioned phenomena that exist within space; because it seeks to realize the enlightenment that is like space; and because it deeply contemplates all sentient beings throughout the entirety of space.

Although this initial generation of the mind may be inferior, the mass of merit from even a single thought-moment is said to be difficult to exhaust; how much more so the merit of generating the mind and practicing for the benefit and happiness of others over many eons!
For what reasons does one resolve the mind [for enlightenment]?
First, by seeing and hearing of the Buddha’s and others’ meritorious powers and spiritual transformations;
second, by hearing the exposition of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka teachings.
Third, seeing and hearing that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, one reflects: "The abiding of the Dharma can extinguish great suffering.

Fourth, during the final age, seeing many sentient beings who are deluded, shameless, stingy, envious, afflicted by sorrow and pain, engaging in evil conduct, negligent, indolent, and lacking faith, one reflects: "When such evil afflictions arise frequently in this turbid world, I shall resolve my mind so that others may follow my example and give rise to the vow for Bodhi. Through this, one then gives rise to the Great Bodhicitta.
When one is about to resolve to generate the bodhicitta, one must first possess ten virtues and give rise to three sublime contemplations.
Regarding the ten superior virtues: first is associating with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).

This means that those whose aspirations and principles accord are considered "near" even if they are distant; conversely, if they do not accord, they are not called virtuous friends even if they are nearby.

Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "A virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) speaks according to the Dharma and acts according to what they have spoken. This means that they themselves do not kill living beings and teach others not to kill;
likewise, they themselves do not hold wrong views and teach others not to hold wrong views—this is called 'acting according to what one has spoken.'"
Furthermore, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is like the moon from the first day to the fifteenth day, because it gradually becomes more perfect and superior.
Second, making offerings to all Buddhas.
This refers to practicing ten kinds of offerings, namely those made in their presence, those made in their absence, and so forth.
Third, the cultivation and accumulation of roots of goodness;
that is, because whatever one does is performed in common with the gathering of virtue.
Fourth, the aspiration to seek the supreme Dharma.
That is to say, one delights in performing supreme wholesome deeds and delights in hearing the supreme Dharma, and so forth.
Fifth, the mind is always gentle and flexible;
that is to say, one’s nature is not fierce or unruly, being like a well-bred horse.
Sixth, the ability to endure suffering:
this means not shrinking from hardships such as cold and heat for the sake of awakening.
Seventh, the profound depth of compassion and loving-kindness.
That is to say, it means to rescue and deliver all beings.
Eighth, the equality of the profound mind:
this means there is no duality between enemy and friend, as one regards the pleasant and the unpleasant with equanimity.
Ninth, faith and delight in the Mahāyāna;
tenth, seeking the Buddha’s wisdom.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains five [of these], as it says: "Furthermore, O sons of the Buddha, with pure minds, supple and of sharp faculties, they have practiced the profound and wondrous path in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas."

The three sublime contemplations are: first, revulsion for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). This means contemplating how one is oppressed by the various sufferings of birth and death, the miserable realms (*durgati*), and the states lacking leisure (*akṣaṇa*); how within one's own body the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) can produce evil karma; how the nine orifices constantly discharge foul and impure substances, being the locus where the thirty-six components arise; how immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*) burn and boil the body and mind; how [the body] is like foam or a bubble, perishing moment by moment; and how, shrouded by ignorance, one creates karma and wanders through the cycle of the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). Thus, through careful and thorough reflection, one develops a deep-seated sense of revulsion and renounces it.

2. Seeking Bodhi. This refers to contemplating the marks and signs of the Buddha’s fruition, his adornment of merit, and the fact that the *dharmakāya* is fundamentally pure, endowed with the aggregates such as morality, the powers, the fearlessnesses, and immeasurable supreme qualities;

it also refers to the accomplishment of the two sublime wisdoms, the compassion for sentient beings, and the guidance of the ignorant and deluded so that they may walk the right path, whereby all classes of sentient beings who encounter him have their afflictions removed. To cultivate and accumulate these qualities is called "seeking."

Third, mindfulness of sentient beings. This means observing that sentient beings are deluded by ignorance and craving, undergoing great and intense suffering; they do not believe in cause and effect, create the causes of evil karma, abandon the Right Path, and instead believe in and accept false paths. They are carried away by the four currents and leaked by the seven outflows. Although they fear various sufferings, they continue to perform evil deeds, constantly bringing upon themselves grief, lamentation, pain, and affliction. They experience the suffering of separation from loved ones, yet upon seeing them again they love them once more; they experience the suffering of encountering those they hate, yet upon awakening from it, their resentment intensifies further.
Seeking to initiate karma, they give rise to suffering without weariness;
seeking pleasure, they violate the precepts, harboring anxiety while indulging in self-indulgence;
committing acts of immediate retribution, they are stubborn and depraved, devoid of shame.

They slander and disparage the Mahāyāna; through deluded attachment they give rise to arrogance. Though possessing intelligence, they have severed their roots of goodness; they are falsely conceited and never repent or reform. Thus they are born into the eight states of no leisure, impoverished of the Dharma and lacking in cultivation.

Although they have heard the teachings, they do not uphold them; instead, they practice perverse deeds and obtain worldly, sublime fruits, claiming to have realized nirvana. Upon the exhaustion of that pleasure, they are reborn once more in the evil realms.
Seeing such beings, one should feel deep compassion from the core of one's heart.

Next, one should resolve to attain enlightenment and make this aspiration: "May I certainly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, and may I be able to bring about every benefit and welfare for all sentient beings."

Alternatively, one may follow one's own inclination regarding the names of the Buddhas, such as the initial aspiration made by Śākyamuni Buddha. As stated in the *Abhidharmakośakārikā*: "During three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), he met, in reverse order, the Victorious Vision (*Vipaśyin*), Dīpaṅkara, Ratnaśikhin, and first, Śākyamuni."

Based on this, Bodhisattva Asaṅga stated: "Through the power of pure supremacy, with a firm mind advancing toward excellence, it is called the Bodhisattva’s initial cultivation during the three incalculable great eons."

First, one arouses the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom to subdue hindrances and defilements; next, one generates great vows so as to constantly encounter virtuous friends as supreme conditions. Even if one meets evil associates who attempt to obstruct and destroy them through skillful means, they never abandon the mind of great bodhi. As the wholesome dharmas they cultivate increase and flourish, they use non-retrogression as their spur; up to this point is called the initial stage of practice.

Having thus initially resolved the mind as described above, one is said to have entered upon unsurpassed bodhi and is included among the ranks of the Mahāyāna bodhisattvas; having set a limit for the ocean of birth and death, one will with courageous resolve surely and swiftly ascend to the other shore.

Now, regarding this "Vast Mind" invoked by the single recitation of the name: it refers to the ten directions being boundless, worlds being boundless, and sentient beings being boundless. Toward such boundless sentient beings, I have, since beginningless time, committed the ten non-virtuous actions; yet now that I have resolved my mind [on enlightenment], I intend to rescue, deliver, and sustain all these beings—therefore, it is called the "Vast Mind," for I desire to liberate them all.

Regarding the statement in the *Asaṅga-śāstra* that these are "distinguished by being subsumed under the spheres of perception (*saṃjñā*) and non-perception (*asaṃjñā*), etc.," this means that these three are taken as objects of contemplation.

"Perception" refers to the seven states with perception; "non-perception" refers to the five states without perception; and "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" excludes the former two. This is the explanation according to the Sarvāstivāda school.

The Mahāyāna commentators explain that the station of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) is called "having perception" (*saṃjñin*), and the station of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is called "without perception" (*asaṃjñin*). As for the third, the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is not "perception" because it is not the aforementioned station of consciousness; nor is it "non-perception" because it is not the aforementioned station of nothingness.
The rest is easy to understand from the treatise (*śāstra*). Furthermore, the treatise asks: "How can those born from eggs and the other three modes of birth enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?

The answer states that there are three causes and conditions. Regarding the phrase "those born in difficult circumstances wait for the [proper] time," the intended meaning of the response is as follows: sentient beings born in difficult circumstances, such as those born from eggs, are permitted to enter [nirvāṇa] once they have emerged from those difficult circumstances; thus, there is no impediment.
"I shall cause all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation.
The commentary states: This is the first resolve.
There are four types of *nirvāṇa*: first, self-nature purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*), which, while still enmeshed in defilements, is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
2. With remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*), meaning the exhaustion of the causes of birth and death;
3. Without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*), meaning the exhaustion of the fruits of birth and death;
4. Non-abiding (*apratisthita*), meaning the direct realization of the two practices of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Alternatively, by adding the purification of nirvāṇa through skillful means, there are five.
This refers to the Bodhisattva’s mental disposition (*āśaya*), which desires that all infinite sentient beings may fully attain *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is called the first mind.
The *Asaṅga-śāstra* states: "Why not speak directly of *nirvāṇa*?

If it were so, it would be no different from the 'expedient *nirvāṇa*' such as the first dhyāna taught by the World-Honored One. This means that the *nirvāṇa* of the first dhyāna and so forth belongs to the mundane path; while it is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) consisting merely in the abandonment of desire, what is spoken of here is the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
Regarding the question, "Why is the realm of *nirvāṇa* with remainder not mentioned?
Because it is a shared fruit," [the answer is: because the *nirvāṇa* without remainder is manifested by the exhaustion of the basis of afflictions and suffering, it is an unshared fruit.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not exclusively," it means that it is not exclusively the basis for the exhaustion of suffering.
Why does the text not mention *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana)?
It is in order to manifest what is common to the three vehicles.
"In this way, although I have brought immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless sentient beings to final nirvana, in reality there are no sentient beings who have attained final nirvana.
The commentary states: This reveals the eternal mind.

This means that the bodhisattva embraces others as himself; when another is liberated, it is as if he himself were liberated. Since there is no "other" outside of himself, he is able to liberate others constantly.
"For what reason? Subhūti!"
"If a bodhisattva has the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span, they are not a bodhisattva.
The commentary states: This is the fourth non-perverted mind.
If the four attachments of "self" and so forth arise, the obstacles of discrimination have not been eliminated, and deluded thoughts thereby increase further; thus, this is perversion.
Since these four attachments are absent, it is called the non-perverted mind.

Medicine is intended fundamentally to eliminate illness; when it lacks efficacy, it instead increases the ailment. Thus, Vasubandhu said: "The notion of 'self' is a collective grasping at the distinctions among the five aggregates throughout the three periods of time. To perceive the continuity of the past self extending to the present without interruption is called the characteristic of a sentient being (*sattva*). To perceive the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as persisting without interruption in the present is called the characteristic of a living being (*jīva*). To perceive the cessation of the life-faculty in the past and its subsequent rebirth within the six realms of existence is called the characteristic of a long-lived being (*āyusmat*)."

However, the Bhagavān stated that "the life-principle is precisely this which is called the mark of a person (*pudgala-nimitta*)," which differs slightly from [the view of] Asaṅga. "Furthermore, Subhūti!"

A bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on anything among phenomena; that is to say, they should not dwell on form when practicing giving, nor should they dwell on sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.
The commentary states: This is based on Vasubandhu’s response to the second question.
However, there are two reasons for designating "generosity" (dāna):
first, it accords with the three meritorious activities of householders; and second, among the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) of those who have left the home life, generosity is the foremost.
Second, its substance is broad and pervasive because it subsumes all six [perfections].
Regarding the three types of meritorious action for householders, they are giving (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
