"Good sons and good daughters who have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should give rise to this thought: 'I should bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.'"
"After having brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, not a single sentient being has actually been brought to parinirvāṇa.
Why is this so, Subhūti?
"If a bodhisattva has the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then they are not a bodhisattva.
[The commentary] states: Vasubandhu says that within this response of the Buddha, first he answers the initial question by citing one corner as an illustration for the remaining two;
second, he explains the contradiction regarding the meaning of non-abiding—this is the first part.

The meaning of this is as follows: Awakening the mind and practicing the path were originally intended to eliminate illness; yet, because the grasping at a self still persists, the illness arises once again.
To ensure that even when one awakens the mind, the "self" is internally eliminated and one does not harbor the thought "I am able," the same applies to practice and the subduing [of afflictions].
Therefore, in answering the first question, the others are intended to be understood by analogy.
However, according to the preceding text, there are likewise four types of mind within this passage. The statement "I should bring [them] to parinirvāṇa" refers to the first mind;
"all sentient beings" refers to the vast mind;
the remaining two may be understood easily by examining the text accordingly.
As Asaṅga’s commentary states, this provides the answers to the first three questions.
Specifically, the phrase "one should give rise to such a thought" answers the first question.

The phrase "having brought all sentient beings to nirvāṇa, yet not a single sentient being has actually been brought to nirvāṇa" answers the second question; that is to say, when delivering sentient beings, one does not give rise to the self-referential grasping of thinking, "I am able to do so."

One must not externally form the perception of sentient beings, nor internally give rise to the grasping of "I"; only when one accords with and conforms to the ultimate truth while delivering sentient beings can it be called true cultivation.

Regarding the statement, "If a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self," this answers the third question: one must realize the principle of the emptiness of both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) so that the two obstacles can be eliminated; only then is it called "subduing. If one says, "I am able," then one is not in accord with the truth.
"Why is that? Subhūti! In truth, there is no dharma whatsoever that sets forth toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this explains the meaning of the non-abiding path as being free from obstacles.

That is to say, when one internally realizes through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) that both self and phenomena are fundamentally empty and utterly non-existent, one does not form the thought "I am able to generate the resolve for enlightenment. Therefore, it is said that there is no agent who generates the resolve for enlightenment by means of a real dharma.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Did the Tathāgata,
while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, obtain any dharma called ‘anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi’?”
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that regarding this second section, there are six parts to the extensive refutation of various doubts.
The first doubt is as follows:

"If it is said that there is truly no dharma named 'Bodhisattva,' how is it that Śākyamuni Tathāgata, at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, made offerings with flowers and spread his hair to cover the mud, thus practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva?"
Second, regarding the passage beginning with "Subhūti!
It is the same for the bodhisattva," the doubt arises as follows:

"If there were no bodhisattvas, the Buddhas would not attain great enlightenment (mahābodhi), and sentient beings would not enter great nirvāṇa, and so forth. If this were the case, for what purpose would a bodhisattva resolve their mind [on awakening] with the desire to lead sentient beings into nirvāṇa and the like?"
These two kinds of doubt arise based on the point where the correct teaching of our own school will be clearly elucidated below.

Furthermore, there are four subsequent doubts that arise from the successive resolution of these [initial] doubts; these will all be explained in their proper place further down. This [present section], therefore, serves to refute the first doubt, and it consists of three parts.
First, it is because they refute the existence of bodhisattvas by harboring slander.

They think: "In reality, there is no dharma that gives rise to the mind of enlightenment; thus, there are no bodhisattvas. How then could the Tathāgata have practiced the conduct of a bodhisattva in the presence of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara?"
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata, at the time of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara," and so forth.
Second, it is for the purpose of eliminating the slander that there are no Buddhas.
The Śāstra states:
"If there were no bodhisattvas, who would attain buddhahood?
In that case, even the Buddhas would not exist.
Therefore, the treatise says:
"If there were no bodhisattvas, there would be no Buddhas.
Such a slanderous claim asserts that there are absolutely no Buddhas.
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas," and so forth.
Third, it is for the purpose of refuting the slander that there is no bodhi.
The Treatise says:
"If there were no Buddhas, then there would be no bodhi to be attained; [it would follow that] the Buddhas do not attain bodhi."
As the sutra states: "The *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* attained by the Tathāgata—within this, there is neither reality nor unreality," and so forth.
Within the preceding section there are three parts: first, the Buddha’s question; second, Subhūti’s answer; and third, the Buddha’s confirmation. This is the initial question.

The Bodhisattva Asaṅga states that this sixteenth [verse] is for the sake of seeking instruction; it corresponds to the twelfth [verse] within the section on "dwelling free from obstacles," which is for the sake of being free from the lack of instruction. This means: since it was previously stated that there is actually no dharma named "Bodhisattva," what would one have sought from Dīpaṃkara Buddha?
Furthermore, because there is no verbal teaching to be sought or heard, this passage exists in order to eliminate this obstacle.
Within this section, there are five textual units.
First, it is for the purpose of avoiding the absence of instruction, as the sūtra says: "The Tathāgata, at the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha," and so forth;

second, it clarifies that bodhi is inexpressible, for the words of Dīpaṃkara Buddha do not correspond to bodhi because they do not accord with verbal expression, as the sūtra says: "If there were any dharma attained by the Tathāgata," and so forth;
third, it explains the meaning of all dharmas being beyond language, as the sūtra says: "The Tathāgata is the very meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas," and so forth.

Fourth, there are those who claim that Śākyamuni did not attain bodhi under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, but attained perfect enlightenment at a later time; in order to eliminate this misconception, it is said in the sutra: "If anyone should say that the Tathāgata attained bodhi," and so forth.
Fifth, it is to demonstrate that true suchness is non-dual; as the sutra says: "Subhūti!"
"Regarding 'that which the Tathāgata has attained,' etc.
Within the preceding section, there are also three parts as categorized by Vasubandhu; this is the first question.

Vasubandhu’s commentary explains that false attachment constitutes "having something attained. When the Tathāgata, under Dīpaṃkara Buddha, gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and realized the principle of the two emptinesses of person and phenomena, he found absolutely nothing attained within what was falsely grasped. Nevertheless, it is through this non-attainment that he attained Bodhi.
Regarding the statement, "Is there any dharma that attains enlightenment?", this means asking Subhūti: "In ultimate reality, is there any dharma that attains enlightenment?
[Subhūti replied: "No, World-Honored One!"
"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no dharma by which the Buddha, while in the presence of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, attained anuttarasamyaksambodhi.
[The commentary] states: This is the second response.
The Buddha said: “So it is, so it is, Subhūti!”
"In truth, there is no dharma that the Tathāgata has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
[The commentary] states: This is the third [point], the accomplishment of the Tathāgata.
Within this, first is the confirmation, followed by the explanation; this is the former.
That is to say, within the principle of *tathatā*, there is nothing to be attained, nor is there any bestowal of prophecy, because both [the self and phenomena] are empty.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "If one receives the prediction of enlightenment by relying on the arising of suchness, suchness has no arising;

if one receives the prediction of enlightenment by relying on the cessation of suchness, suchness has no cessation," and so forth. This is because within the manifestation of true suchness (*tathatā*), there is no prediction of enlightenment. It merely means that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no substantial dharma that can give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment; it does not mean that the true wisdom capable of conforming to bodhi—thereby being named bodhi—is also non-existent. Therefore, in terms of phenomenal reality (*saṃvṛti*), bodhi is certainly not absent.

As Asaṅga says: "When one is in perfect accord with reality, no dharma can be apprehended; therefore, it is said that there is no dharma by which one may generate the resolve for enlightenment. This does not refer to the realm of conventional phenomena, nor does it mean that there are no verbal teachings to be heard."
“Subhūti! If there were any dharma that the Tathāgata had attained as anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have bestowed upon me this prediction:
‘In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni.’”

The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this second section is the "explanation and establishment," which has two parts: first, the "refutation and clarification," and second, the "conformative establishment. This is the former.
That is to say, if one were to attain bodhi through any dharma associated with the lighting of a lamp, this would constitute "attainment";
that which is attained is what is grasped as existing;
because of grasping at existence, one does not accord with True Suchness (tathatā).
"One who does not accord with True Suchness (tathatā) is of the class of ordinary beings; how then can you bestow a prediction of enlightenment upon me?
It is only by realizing True Suchness through the mind that one finds nothing at all to be obtained within the two objects of self and phenomena;
because there is nothing to be obtained, it is called 'accordance' or 'convergence' with the True."
Because one accords with reality, the two types of grasping are entirely exhausted;

since grasping is exhausted, one is able to attain Buddhahood, which is why Dīpaṃkara bestowed the prediction of enlightenment upon me—knowing that my realization of reality was without anything to be attained.
As Asaṅga says: "This is the second [point]: the words of Dīpaṃkara do not refer to bodhi; it should not be accepted according to the literal expression.
Within this, there are two parts: first, an explanation by way of negation (paryudāsa), and second, an establishment by way of affirmation (vidhi); this is the former.

He thought: "The Tathāgata Śākyamuni did not attain enlightenment by taking the words of Dīpaṃkara literally; this is because wisdom realizes the truth through non-apprehension. If enlightenment could be described by Dīpaṃkara and Śākyamuni had grasped it according to those words, he would possess discriminative attachment and his mind would not have accorded with reality. How then could Dīpaṃkara have bestowed a prediction of enlightenment upon me?"
Because I attained realization not by means of words, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara bestowed upon me this prediction, saying:
"In a future age, you shall become a buddha named Śākyamuni. For there is, in truth, no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it was for this reason that the Buddha Dīpaṃkara granted me the prediction, speaking these words.
The commentary states: This is the second [point], which establishes [the argument] in accordance with the truth. Why is this so?
Because "Tathāgata" has the meaning of the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena.
The commentary states: This second passage by Vasubandhu is intended to eliminate doubts regarding the denial of the Buddha’s existence.
Within it, the first part clarifies that the Dharmakāya exists, while the subsequent part refutes false claims; this is the former.
It is said that there may be doubt, thinking:
"If there are no bodhisattvas and no one attains buddhahood, then the Buddha must also not exist.
To dispel this doubt, it is stated that there is the Dharma-Buddha (*dharmabuddha*).
Due to the deluded attachments of sentient beings, they take the five aggregates to be the self;

the wise, however, understand that these are subject to rapid decay and destruction, possessing no reality whatsoever. There is only the True Principle, which is both eternal and true. It is eternal because it remains as it is, without change or alteration;
it is true because it is free from delusion and is not inverted.

This ultimate truth cannot be harmed by water or fire, nor can it be destroyed by wind or thieves; whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, its nature remains eternally as it is, and whether it is taught or not, its meaning does not change.
However, because ordinary beings are deluded and inverted, they cling to the body as being the self and fail to contemplate the principle of the body, remaining submerged in saṃsāra for a long time.

The noble ones possess correct knowledge; thus, they do not attach to the body but contemplate only the true principle. Being able to realize this, birth and death are forever extinguished and the veil of delusion is completely exhausted. Because the principle is now manifest, they are called Tathāgatas.
By this, it is clarified that it is not the case that there is no Buddha.
As Asanga states: "This is the third [point], the explanation of the meaning of being beyond words.
That is to say, for what reason are those dharmas not explained separately?"
It is said that the root of all dharmas is essential in principle and yet pure; it becomes true only when wisdom accords with it, for it cannot be realized through verbal explanations.
"If anyone says that the Tathāgata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, that person speaks untruth."
The commentary states: This is a refutation of false discourse.
First, it refutes the words of others; second, it establishes that there is nothing to be attained. This is the first [point].
Since the Tathāgata is True Suchness (tathatā), how could he be described by means of verbal expression as being real?
Therefore, if one were to speak [of it], that would be untrue speech, for it is merely a conceptual construction.
Asasaṅga says: This fourth [point] refutes external doubts. The doubt is as follows:
This is for the purpose of severing the grasping that [claims]: "Śākyamuni did not attain bodhi under Dīpaṃkara, but attained it later by himself.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the rejection of that external grasping; second, the self-manifestation of non-attainment.
Since there is no dharma that can be apprehended, how could there be a subsequent taking for oneself?
Therefore, such speech is called "unreal.
In this current version of the sutra, the characters "unreal speech" (不實語) have been omitted, though they appear in all other editions.
"Subhūti! In truth, there is no dharma that the Buddha has attained as *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Commentary states: This is the second passage.
“Subhūti! The anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi attained by the Tathāgata—within it there is neither reality nor unreality.
[The Commentary] states: This is the third passage of Vasubandhu.
Within this, first, the doubts and attachments of outsiders are refuted; second, the analogy is presented to manifest the nature of the body. In the former [section], there are three parts:

first, it clarifies that what is attained is neither real nor unreal; second, it reveals that this Dharma is attained only by the Buddha; third, it provides a summary conclusion. This is the first [of those three].

As Asaṅga states, this constitutes the fifth section clarifying the meaning of the non-duality of *tathatā* (suchness). It contains three parts: first, clarifying that *tathatā* is both dependent upon and transcendent from verbal expression; second, demonstrating that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and phenomena themselves (*dharma*) are attained only by the Buddha; and third, a concluding summary. This is the first part.

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: There are those who slanderously claim, "The Tathāgata did not attain bodhi. To sever this doubt, it is said that "the bodhi attained by the Tathāgata is neither real nor unreal. This means that because the Tathāgata has attained that bodhi, it is called "not unreal";
yet, because it does not possess the characteristics of being a truly existent conditioned phenomenon, it is called "not real."
As Asaṅga’s commentary states: it is not real because it cannot be grasped according to the literal expression;
yet it is not false because it is not to be sought apart from expression.
The speech of ordinary beings is false and delusive, and is therefore not real.
The teachings of the Buddhas are reliable and therefore not false;
the words of ordinary people cannot be attained and are therefore unreal;
yet because they rely upon the Buddha’s words to be explained, they are not false.
If one seeks [awakening] apart from words, then awakening would be without cause, which is termed "unreal.
Because it must rely upon hearing the teachings to be realized, awakening has a cause, which is termed "not false."
If one were to grasp at things according to their literal expression, there would be no escape from birth and death; therefore, one must not rely on the literal expression.
Yet, to accord with the Dharma, one must necessarily rely on words before one can harmonize with the Truth.
"However, by practicing in accordance with the Buddha’s words, one will realize it spontaneously at the time of later realization.
For this reason, the Tathāgata said: 'All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma.
The commentary states: This second point clarifies that the Dharma is attained only by the Buddha.
"All phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) refers to the fundamental essence of the myriad dharmas of ultimate truth; thus they are called "all.
"All are the Buddha-dharma" means that this is realized solely by the Buddha, as others cannot attain it.
“Subhūti! That which is called ‘all dharmas’ is precisely not all dharmas; therefore it is named ‘all dharmas.
[The commentary] states: This is the third [section], the summary and conclusion.
"To speak of 'all dharmas' refers to the dharmas realized by the Buddha;
'they are not all dharmas' means they are not the dharmas attained by others, nor are they dharmas characterized by conceptual discrimination."
“Subhūti! It is as if, for example, there were a person whose body was tall and large. Subhūti said:
“World-Honored One!
When the Tathāgata speaks of a person’s body as large, it is not a large body; it is merely named a ‘large body.
The commentary states: Vasubandhu’s *Bhāṣya* explains that this second point cites a metaphor to illustrate the nature of the body.
First, the Buddha presents a simile; second, Subhūti confirms it accordingly.
That which is called "long" is a metaphor for the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), as other sūtras also refer to it as "wondrous";
that which is "great" is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
These two types of bodies are attained respectively by being free from the two obstacles of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
When it is said that "the human body is long and great," this refers to the two bodies of Dharma (*dharmakāya*) and Retribution (*vipākakāya*).
"Then it is not a great body" means that it is not a body produced by various false conceptualizations and discriminations.

Wuzhuo’s commentary states: From this point onward is the seventeenth [stage], for the purpose of entering the path of realization; furthermore, among the eight stations of dwelling, this is the fifth, the station of the pure mind. This means that while the sixteen aforementioned distinctions—the four stations of dwelling belonging to the stage of practice through faith—are cultivated by ordinary beings prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) over one *kalpa*, this is the station of the pure mind, which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas of the ten stages.

Within this, the first part demonstrates the attainment of wisdom at the time of entering the path of realization; thus, from the passage "The bodhisattva is also like this" onwards, it clarifies the abandonment of pride, of which this is the first instance.
This refers to the bodhisattva who has entered the stages obtaining two kinds of wisdom: first, the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); second, the wisdom of equality.
If one obtains this wisdom, one is born into the family of the Tathāgatas and attains the certainty of succeeding to the Buddha-lineage; this is the wisdom that encompasses the spiritual lineage.

That is to say, the pure dharma-realm is the abode of the Buddha and is called the "family of the Tathāgata. When Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages realize and accord with it through non-conceptual wisdom, this is described as "birth."
In this way, such bodhisattvas are certain to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas; therefore, it is called the "knowledge that encompasses the lineage.

It should be understood that because bodhisattvas prior to the stages have not yet been born into the family of the Tathāgatas, although they are indeed sons of the Buddha, they are somewhat distant from him and thus are not said to succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas.

Although those of the two vehicles are also children of the Buddha, because they seek only their own benefit and are thus incapable of succeeding [to the lineage], the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* describes the śrāvaka as being like the son of an ignorant maidservant.

Although all ordinary beings are likewise embraced by the Buddha, protected by him, and equally the object of his compassion, because they have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment, they are not yet capable of succeeding him.
Only Bodhisattvas who have entered the stages (*bhūmi*) are born directly from the true *dharmadhātu*, and thus are capable of succeeding to the lineage of the Buddhas.

The treatise states: "If one has long aspired to be born into this family, once born there, one obtains that body; this is called the 'wondrous body' (*sūkṣmakāya*). This means that because Bodhisattvas prior to the stages have diligently and earnestly made such aspirations for a long night, they enter the first stage and thereby obtain the wondrous body.

Furthermore, there are five kinds of causes and conditions for the equality of wisdom. First is the equality of coarseness and evil: having entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), one has already abandoned the female body, the eighth existence, and the three evil destinies; therefore, all are equal.
Second is the equality of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which refers to attaining the principle of equality through the two kinds of emptiness.

Third is the equality of the associated with abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃprayukta*), which means that the nature of abandonment is itself the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) attained; it is called the equality associated with abandonment because it is associated with such abandonment.

Fourth is the equality associated with the mind free from expectation. This means that prior to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), when one trains in contemplating *tathatā* (suchness), there is still desire and expectation;
however, once one has entered the first stage (*bhūmi*) and realized the true *dharmadhātu*, one becomes associated with the equality realized by the mind free from expectation.

Fifth, the equality of the realized path of all Bodhisattvas: this means that just as the various currents of a hundred rivers ultimately merge into the stillness of the great ocean, so too, although the myriad practices differ, upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), they all equally realize the true great ocean.
Because one attains this equality, one is said to possess the "Great Body" (mahākāya).
The commentary explains: that which attains the wisdom of encompassing the spiritual lineage is called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body);
because it attains equality, it is called the *dharmakāya* (Dharma Body).
The "wondrous body" and the "great body" serve as analogies for these two respectively. "Subhūti!
It is the same for a bodhisattva: if they should say, 'I shall bring immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa,' then they are not called a bodhisattva."
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this constitutes the second section, which resolves doubts, and it contains three parts.

First, a doubt arises regarding the fundamental tenet: namely, since it was previously stated that there is no dharma that gives rise to the bodhicitta, if the Bodhisattva does not exist, then there should likewise be no one to attain enlightenment as a Bodhisattva;
and if sentient beings do not exist, whom would one teach and transform so as to lead them into nirvana?
If there were no bodhisattvas, who would adorn the pure lands?

Second, this arises from the dispelling of doubt: it is taught that the bodhisattva does not perceive others as sentient beings, nor does he perceive himself as existing as a bodhisattva, and so forth. This is because the Tathāgata does not perceive them; thus they are said to be "without sentient beings" and so on.
Is it because sentient beings and the like do not truly exist that the Buddha does not see them?
Third, there may be doubt, saying:
"It was previously stated that the mind abides in inversion; if this is so, then merit is also inverted. If it is inverted, how can it be called a wholesome dharma?"

Because of this doubt, as stated in the sutra, "If there were a world-system of three thousand great thousand worlds filled with the seven treasures," and so forth, there are three doubts regarding the beginning:
first, that if there were no bodhisattvas, the Buddhas would not attain enlightenment;
second, that if there were no sentient beings, they would not enter nirvana.
Third, if there were no bodhisattvas, there would also be no adornment and purification of Buddha-lands.
This explains the first two doubts; herein, the first part provides the thesis and the second part provides the explanation—this is the former.

The meaning of this is as follows: If a bodhisattva clings to the thought, "I shall attain enlightenment" or "there are distinct sentient beings to be delivered," they are not called a bodhisattva, because of the presence of the notions of self, person, and so forth;
if that were the case, how could they ever attain enlightenment?
Can one cause sentient beings to enter nirvana?

This is because there are only conventionally designated sentient beings; for example, it is as if an illusory person were to preach the Dharma to another illusory person. Since there is only a conventionally designated sentient being formed by the aggregation of the five aggregates, they may attain nirvana without remainder. However, because there is no such thing as a real sentient being as one might grasp at, one does not perceive any sentient being who attains extinction.

This means that because there are provisional bodhisattvas who seek realization, the Buddhas attain enlightenment; yet, since there is no grasping at a truly existent enlightenment, there is likewise no bodhisattva.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle thirteen, states: "The five aggregates combine and are designated as 'so-and-so. Ordinary people claim that this 'so-and-so' exists substantially;
however, a person of wisdom understands that among the aggregates there is no such name as 'so-and-so,' and apart from the aggregates, there is likewise no such name as 'so-and-so.'"

"Why is this? Subhūti, there is truly no dharma that can be called a 'bodhisattva. Therefore, the Buddha says that all dharmas are without self, without person, without sentient being, and without life-span."
The commentary states: This is the second explanation.

Regarding the phrase "there is no dharma named 'Bodhisattva,'" it means that if there were actual dharmas, all would constitute sentient beings by virtue of those dharmas, and thus could be called "Bodhisattvas";
since dharmas lack any actual reality, there is likewise no Bodhisattva to be constituted.

Regarding the statement, "The Buddha taught that all phenomena are without self or person," this means that at the time of realizing the truth, one penetrates the principle of non-self and perceives neither the grasping at a person nor the grasping at phenomena; therefore, such a person is a bodhisattva.

As Asaṅga says: "The preceding analogies, such as the 'wonderful body' and the 'great body,' demonstrate the entry into and realization of the Path. This constitutes the second [section], clarifying the departure from pride (*māna*).
Specifically, prior to entering the stages (*bhūmi*), one obstructs the non-abiding path by thinking, 'I am able to practice,' and so forth.

Once having entered the stages and beyond, one realizes the equality of the two kinds of emptiness within the *dharmadhātu*; all conceptualizations of self and phenomena entirely vanish, and the pride of 'I can' is forever absent; hence it is called 'departing from pride.'"

The Treatise states: "If a bodhisattva harbors the notion of sentient beings, they will not attain the wondrous body or the great body. Regarding this, "the wondrous body" refers to the attainment of the perfection of the body, because the body achieves ultimate transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*);
"the great body" refers to the fact that the bodies of all sentient beings are subsumed within one's own body.
The Master said: "The transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) refers precisely to the attainment of bodhi and nirvāṇa. 'Subhūti!
If a bodhisattva were to say, "I shall adorn the buddha-fields," he cannot be called a bodhisattva.'"
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this refutes doubt.
Specifically, there is a doubt that says: "If there were no bodhisattvas, one should not purify the buddha-fields."
Within this, there are two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation. This is the first. The meaning is as follows:

if one wishes to adorn and purify a Buddha-land, one must necessarily adorn and purify one’s own mind. By listening to the sutras, studying wisdom, realizing the true principle of the Dharma, and eliminating the two obstacles, the internal mind becomes pure, and consequently, the external land also becomes pure.

Thus, it is because Śikhin perceived purity while Śāriputra beheld impurity that we know: it is solely due to the differences between defilement and purity within their inner minds that the external lands also appear as two distinct states of purity and impurity.

Therefore, for one who would purify a Buddha-field, they must first eliminate the two attachments to self and phenomena; because the conceptualization of self and phenomena has ceased, they possess internal adornment and dwell externally amidst the seven treasures.

If one says, "I shall adorn [the Buddha-fields]," this indicates that the grasping at a self has not yet been extinguished; such a person is not called a bodhisattva. Therefore, the treatise states: "When wisdom practices the penetration of consciousness-only."
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* states that because the mind is pure,
[the land is pure], and it further states that patience, ethical discipline, and the ten paths of wholesome action are the bodhisattva’s pure land.
"Why is this? What the Tathāgata calls the adornment of Buddha-lands is in fact no adornment; it is merely designated as 'adornment. The commentary states:

Within this second explanation there are two parts. First, it clarifies that signlessness (*animitta*) is true adornment; second, it clarifies that one who realizes this principle is a true Bodhisattva. This is the first part.
"What the Tathāgata calls 'adornment' refers to the adornment of signlessness;
'it is not an adornment' means it is not the adornment of signs;
'it is called adornment' refers to true adornment."
“Subhūti! If a bodhisattva penetrates the non-existence of self and phenomena, the Tathāgata calls him a true bodhisattva.
The commentary states: This is the second passage.
That is to say, if a bodhisattva realizes the emptiness of self and phenomena and realizes the principle of non-self, they are a true bodhisattva and possess true adornment;
if there were a self or phenomena, one would fundamentally not be a bodhisattva, nor would there be any adornment.
Asuṅga states: "From this point downward, all seek the Buddha-ground.

This means that from here until the end of the sutra, within the categories of distinctions, this is the eighteenth; among the dwelling places, it is the sixth, the ultimate dwelling place; and among the three grounds, it is the third, the Buddha-ground.
Among these, there are six: first, the perfection of the purity of the land, as in the sutra: "If a bodhisattva should say, 'I shall adorn [it],' and so forth";
second, the perfection of unsurpassed vision and wisdom, as in the sutra: "Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye? and so forth;
third, the perfection of the body with its secondary marks, as in the sutra: "Can the Buddha be seen by means of the perfected form-body? and so forth.
Fourth is the perfection of the body of marks, as in the sutra: "Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his perfected marks?
Fifth is the perfection of speech, as in the sutra: "Do not say that the Tathāgata has such a thought," and so forth;
sixth is the perfection of mind, as in the sutra: "Are there any sentient beings in future ages... and so forth; this is the first [of these six].

The meaning of this is as follows: it refers to the bodhisattvas who, having perfected their cultivation through the ten preceding stages (*bhūmi*), have eliminated the dualistic attachments to persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*) and realized the *dharmakāya* of enlightenment; this is termed "the perfection of the purity of the land."

Within the Chinese text, there are four sections: first, for the sake of the perfection of the purity of the buddha-field through *samāpatti*, as in the sutra passage beginning, "If a bodhisattva should say... and so forth;
second, for the sake of severing that [misconception], the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is established, as in the sutra passage beginning, "The Tathāgata speaks of adornment...
and so forth; third, for the sake of the two kinds of selflessness, as in the sutra passage, "If a bodhisattva penetrates selflessness and the selflessness of phenomena... and so forth.
Fourth, for the sake of attaining the two kinds of perfect awakening regarding those two kinds of selflessness, as the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata calls him a true Bodhisattva."
How are these demonstrated? If one says, "I have accomplished this," that is the grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-ātma-grāha*);
to "adorn the buddha-field" is the grasping at a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātma-grāha*).
"This one is not a bodhisattva. "Subhūti,
what do you think?"
“Does the Tathāgata possess the fleshly eye?
“It is so, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the fleshly eye.”
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this refutes the second doubt.
There is a doubt which asks:
"Why is it that it was previously stated that a bodhisattva does not perceive others as sentient beings, does not perceive himself as a bodhisattva, and does not perceive a pure buddha-field?"
"Is it because all phenomena do not exist that they are not seen, or is it because the Buddhas themselves do not see?

This passage contains two parts: first, it clarifies that the Buddha possesses the capacity to see by explaining the five kinds of eyes; second, from "As among the sands of the Ganges... onwards, it clarifies that there is something to be seen.

The five eyes in the preceding section constitute five distinct segments; within each, first is the Buddha’s question, followed by Subhūti’s response. This initial segment clarifies the existence of the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*).

As Asaṅga states: "From this point downward is the second [section], for the sake of the perfection of the purity of supreme vision and wisdom. Within this, there are three parts: first, to clarify the perfection of the purity of supreme vision, it is taught that the Buddha possesses the five eyes;
next, from "As in the Ganges River" onward, to clarify the perfection of the purity of supreme wisdom, it is taught that the Buddha knows the minds of sentient beings;
finally, from "If there were a person who filled... onward, to clarify the perfection of mastery over merit.
The first five eyes constitute five sections, which may be understood as previously explained.
An external doubt arises:
"It was previously stated that the internal realization of ultimate truth through non-conceptual wisdom constitutes true adornment; [how then can these eyes be considered such?]"

When the ultimate truth is realized through external signs, none of these are perceived at all; that is to say, the Buddha perceives reality solely with the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) and possesses no other eyes.
To explain this point, it is said that the Buddha possesses five eyes; such is the intended meaning of the treatise.

Furthermore, the treatise states: "Within this, there is a brief explanation of four kinds of eyes: namely, those comprised by form, those comprised by the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), those comprised by conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and those comprised by all aspects of all that is to be known."

The inclusion within form (*rūpa*) is further twofold, namely: the fruit of the Dharma (*dharmaphala*) and the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*). These constitute the coarse objects of the five eyes; thus, they are the first category of inclusion within form. The commentary explains:

The two eyes—the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) and the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*)—have the sense-faculty of form (*rūpindriya*) as their nature, meaning they are produced from the four great elements of pure form (*rūpaprasāda*).

Whether they are of the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) or nurtured growth (*aupacayika*), they are termed the "fleshly eye. This refers to the fruit of the Dharma; it is common to other realms and the four dhyānas.

If one attains it by practicing dhyāna and eliminating hindrances, this is called the fruit of cultivation; it exists only within the stages of the four dhyānas, meaning that one is able to see all forms—internally and externally, on both sides, inside and out, above and below.
The treatise states: "Because of the power of the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-jñāna-bala*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) functions without inversion;

therefore, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is subsumed as preceding [conventional truth]. Within this, one preaches the Dharma for others; if that Dharma is established for that person, this wisdom is called the 'Dharma-eye' (*dharma-cakṣus*). This means that it is necessary to observe the principle through the "wisdom-eye" (*prajñā-cakṣus*);
the Dharma-eye knows the capacities of beings and preaches the Dharma, thereby preaching for others without error.

This means that what is signified (*vācya*), the signifier (*vācaka*), the observation of principles (*tattva*), the observation of phenomena (*vastu*), the observation of principles, and the knowledge of capacities (*indriya*) correspond, in order, to wisdom (*prajñā*) and the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).
The *Śāstra* states: "The effortless wisdom regarding all aspects within all that should be known is called the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*)."

Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva spoke of these in terms of distinctions among persons: that which exists in ordinary beings is called the "flesh eye" or the "divine eye"; in those of the Two Vehicles, it is called the "wisdom eye"; in Bodhisattvas, it is called the "dharma eye"; and in the Tathāgata, it is called the "buddha eye. This interpretation is likewise without fault.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the divine eye?”
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the divine eye. "Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
Does the Tathāgata possess the wisdom-eye?
"It is so, World-Honored One!"
“The Tathāgata possesses the wisdom-eye. “Subhūti,
what do you think?”
“Does the Tathāgata possess the Dharma-eye?
“Indeed he does, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata possesses the Dharma-eye.”
“Subhūti, what do you think? Does the Tathāgata possess the Buddha-eye?”
“Thus it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata possesses the Buddha-eye.
The commentary states: this clarifies that he possesses the latter four eyes; the explanation of their meaning is as above.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Regarding all the grains of sand in the Ganges River, does the Buddha say that they are sand?”
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that the preceding section explained that the Tathāgata possesses the five eyes, thereby clarifying his capacity for vision;

from here on, it clarifies the various distinctions among sentient beings and further demonstrates that there is indeed something seen. This means that although there are no truly existent sentient beings as imagined by the *parikalpita-svabhāva*, they can still be saved and perceived; it is not the case that these conventionally designated sentient beings are perceived without causes and conditions.

Although there is no acting condition (*kāraṇa-pratyaya*), a functional condition (*vṛtti-pratyaya*) can still be found; that is to say, because one does not perceive the substantially real person (*pudgala*) or phenomena (*dharma*) as they are grasped by others within the context of cause and effect, and because these cannot be apprehended, they are termed the "emptiness of sentient beings and the realm."

It is not that the Buddha lacks eyes and thus does not see, nor is it that there are truly no sentient beings to be seen; rather, it is because of those causes and conditions consisting of inverted, false, and provisional phenomena.

Within this section, there are five parts: first, the Buddha asks about the sands of the Ganges; second, Subhūti answers that they are such sands; third, he uses the sands of the Ganges as a metaphor to pose a question; fourth, Subhūti answers that they are very many; and fifth, the Buddha elaborates on the completion [of the analogy]. This is the first.
As Asaṅga says: "The foregoing establishes the 'view' for the sake of realizing that which is to be known;
it establishes the 'knower' for the sake of teaching various sentient beings how to pacify their minds."

This means that because the fleshly eye and the divine eye serve as their precursors, one gives rise to the wisdom-eye and the Dharma-eye to contemplate principles and discern capacities, thereby preaching the Dharma for others.

What was previously described as the purity of vision (*darśana-viśuddhi*) was intended to manifest realization (*sākṣātkriyā*); what is now described as the purity of knowledge (*jñāna-viśuddhi*) is intended to manifest instruction (*avavāda*).

That is to say, among sentient beings, whether they possess a mind of attachment or a mind free from attachment, the Tathāgata perceives and knows them all, providing instruction so that they may abandon defilement and advance toward virtue.
Regarding the question, "Does the Buddha say that all sand is sand?", it asks whether, among the sand of causes and conditions, the Buddha says it is a grasped, substantial sand.
The meaning of the question is as follows:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata has said that this is sand."
The commentary states: This is the second answer. "Subhūti, what do you think?"

Suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in a single Ganges River; and suppose there were as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in all those Ganges Rivers—would these not be very numerous?
The commentary states: This third point relies on the analogy of grains of sand to illustrate abundance.
That is to say, this merely cites a small portion for the sake of illustration; in reality, sentient beings are without limit and are not restricted to only as many as those grains of sand.
"Very much so, World-Honored One!
This is the fourth passage. The Buddha said to Subhūti:
"In all those lands, the Tathāgata fully knows the various kinds of minds of all sentient beings.
The commentary states: This constitutes the fifth accomplishment of the Tathāgata.
Within this, there is first the heading and secondly the explanation; this is the former.

"Various kinds of mind" refers to the differentiated and inverted minds of the six consciousnesses; because all deluded minds are inverted, and because they are divorced from true mindfulness, they are termed "inverted."
"Those who are divorced from true mindfulness" refers to those who have abandoned the four foundations of mindfulness; thus they are said to not abide in that true wisdom.
The Tathāgata fully knows such states of mind as these.

As Asaṅga says: "Regarding the various kinds of mind, one should know there are two types: namely, the defiled and the pure; that is to say, the mind associated with desire and the mind free from desire. Because the Tathāgata knows the minds of such sentient beings as described, and because he instructs them all to sever evil and give rise to good, it is called the purity of wisdom.
The Treatise says: "Wisdom is established in order to bring about the tranquility of the minds of various sentient beings.
Why is this? The Tathāgata has taught that all minds are 'non-minds'; it is precisely for this reason they are called 'minds'."
The commentary states: In this explanation, first, it clarifies that the inverted mind is not true abiding; second, it reveals the characteristics of delusion. This is the first [point].
"When the Tathāgata speaks of 'all minds' as abiding," this refers to the deluded mind;

"all are non-minds" means they are not the truly abiding mind, for abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness is called true abiding, and abiding in the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) is called true abiding;
"this is called mind" refers to this deluded and inverted mind.
Asuṅga said: "In this [section on] the purity of wisdom, it is stated that 'the abiding of the mind is itself the non-abiding of the mind.
Likewise, why is it not stated in the [section on] the purity of vision that 'the eye is itself the non-eye'?"
"Because of abiding in a single state, and because after the purification of vision and wisdom one establishes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the beginning is also accomplished.

The commentary says: Since the mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is initially false but can later become true, within the purification of wisdom it is said that the mind abides and yet does not abide. However, once the Buddha-eye is attained, it is perfectly fulfilled; since there is no further distinction between before and after or any shifting difference, it is not said that the eye is "not the eye."
The meaning of this passage is difficult to understand according to the treatise.
Why is this so? Subhūti!
"The past mind cannot be apprehended, the present mind cannot be apprehended, and the future mind cannot be apprehended.

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "This demonstrates that their continuity is inverted. This means: "Because it is past and future, it cannot be apprehended; because the present mind consists of false conceptualization, it cannot be apprehended. Thus, it is shown that the abiding of that mind is inverted and all consciousnesses are false, as they are observed through the [three] time periods."
As Asanga said: "The past and the future are so called because they have already ceased and have not yet arisen;
the present is so called because it is the primary reality (paramārtha). Subhūti!"
"What do you think?
If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would that person, by reason of this, acquire much merit?"
The commentary states: Vasubandhu’s explanation says that this constitutes the second section of the third textual unit.
That is to say, there is further doubt:
"If it was previously stated that the mind abides in perversion, then if this is so, merit (*puṇya*) would also be perverted."
"If this is inverted, why is it called a wholesome dharma?

To sever this doubt, [the Buddha] demonstrates that although the mind's dwelling may be inverted, the merit practiced is not so; for this is the root of the Buddha’s wisdom. Because when practicing giving one does not cling to the self and so forth, but seeks only unsurpassed bodhi, the merit is therefore exceedingly great.
In this passage, first the Buddha asks, second Subhūti answers, and finally the Tathāgata confirms; this is the first part.

That is to say, if one were to give away the seven precious treasures and so forth for the sake of seeking the Prajñāpāramitā, and by hearing, studying, and practicing it, were to attain Buddhahood, the merit thereof would be exceedingly great.

Asuṅga states that this refers to the third aspect within the purity of wisdom of unsurpassed vision: the fulfillment of mastery over merit. This means that by practicing generosity and other virtues for the sake of prajñā, the qualities of merit are brought to completion.
"So it is, World-Honored One!
By these causes and conditions, this person gains exceedingly great merit.
The commentary states: This is the second answer.
“Subhūti! If merit were substantial, the Tathāgata would not say that one acquires a great deal of merit;
because merit is non-substantial, the Tathāgata says that one acquires a great deal of merit.”
The commentary states: This is the third [point] concerning the accomplishment of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the phrase "if merit were real," this means that if one were to say that practicing generosity for the sake of wisdom is as truly existent as practicing generosity for the sake of one's own body, the Buddha would not say that such a person attains great merit.

Because one practices giving with the three aspects of emptiness, it differs from practicing giving while being attached to its karmic rewards; for this reason, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.

By this standard, one should understand that the previous comparison—where giving wealth, life, and so forth was found to fall short of receiving and upholding this sutra—is because those [former acts] cannot eliminate signs and do not seek bodhi.
This means that if, at the time of sacrificing one's body and life, it benefits only a few starving beings and cannot bring about extensive benefit;
whereas if one upholds the Prajñāpāramitā, one shall attain Buddhahood and bring salvation and benefit to a vast multitude—therefore, its merit is superior.
If one speaks of it from a horizontal perspective, the suffering of casting off the body is extreme;
yet from a vertical perspective, it does not equal the merit of upholding this sutra. "Subhūti!..."
"What do you think?
Can the Buddha be seen by means of his complete physical body?

Vasubandhu states that the preceding section has finished refuting doubts regarding the original locus; from here on, there are four further doubts, which arise because each subsequent doubt is raised to resolve the one before it.
This constitutes the third major section, which refutes doubts; it is the first of the three sub-sections within that [third] major section.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, the doubt that the body endowed with marks and signs is the Buddha.
Second, from "Do not say this" onwards, there is doubt that the Buddha has spoken [thus];
third, from "Are there any sentient beings" onwards, there is doubt that there are no people who believe.
This is the first [point].
It is asked in doubt:

"If the Buddhas are designated by the name 'Buddha' because of their unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), how is it that the Buddhas are called 'Buddhas' despite having accomplished the eighty secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*) and the thirty-two major marks (*lakṣaṇa*)?"
The commentary explains: This refers to the doubt arising regarding the statement previously made about the Tathāgata—that is, the true suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the refutation of doubts concerning the form-body (*rūpakāya*).
Next, the doubt regarding the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) is refuted.
This section further consists of two parts: first, the Buddha’s question; second, Subhūti’s response. This is the former.
The intent of the question is as follows:
"Can the Dharma-body Buddha be seen through the beautiful form of the Reward-body?
And can the Dharma-body Buddha be seen by means of the physical body with its halo extending one fathom and its various secondary marks?"
Asuṅga stated: "This third [category] is for the sake of the perfection of the body with its secondary marks (anuvyañjana).
The intent of the question is as follows:

"Because the Buddha acts according to the capacities of beings, there exist the bodies of retribution and transformation endowed with secondary marks; yet within the Dharma of ultimate truth, there is also the excellence of the non-differentiation of the nature of form. Now, I ask: can one perceive the distinct secondary marks of the Dharma-body?"
"This text exists for the purpose of causing sentient beings to internally realize the perfection of the Dharma-body and externally to obtain a body endowed with excellent physical marks.
[The interlocutor replied: 'No, World-Honored One!'"
"One should not see the Tathāgata by means of the body of perfected form.
The commentary states: In this second response, first there is the thesis, followed by the explanation; this is the first [part].
"Why is this? That which the Tathāgata calls the 'complete physical body' is not a complete physical body; it is merely designated as the 'complete physical body.
The commentary states: This is the explanation.
"When the Tathāgata speaks of 'the body endowed with the marks of physical perfection,' this refers to the bodies of reward and transformation, along with their minor marks;
'it is not a body endowed with the marks of physical perfection' means it is not the body of physical perfection consisting of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā);
'this is called the body endowed with the marks of physical perfection' refers to the bodies of reward and transformation."

As Asaṅga says: "The forms of the reward-body and the transformation-body manifest according to the capacities of beings and possess physical excellence; yet internally, one realizes the signless and possesses the excellent color-nature of the Dharma-body. Because one internally realizes the Dharma-nature body, the external body endowed with physical excellence is fully perfected. Nevertheless, the body endowed with physical excellence is not itself the Dharma-nature-perfected body."
This means that the Dharma-body is like space: although it has no form or characteristics, it manifests a vast and translucent reflection within a mirror;
the Dharma-body is likewise, for although it has no form or characteristics, it manifests the Reward-body and Transformation-bodies within the Mirror-like Wisdom.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of his possession of the various marks?”
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this second [section] refutes doubts regarding the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
Within it, there is first the question and next the answer; this is the former.
The questioner’s intent was:
"Can one perceive the Dharma-body, the signless Buddha, by means of the thirty-two marks?
Asaṅga replied: "This fourth [point] is for the sake of the perfection of the Body of Marks."
The question means:

"The Buddha has three bodies, namely the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body. While the Reward-body and the Transformation-body possess thirty-two marks of distinction, does the Dharma-body also possess the marks of non-distinctive dharmatā?"
"Now I ask: can the Dharma-body be seen by means of its distinctive marks and signs?
"No, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata should not be seen by means of the possession of all marks."
The commentary states: This is the initial thesis within the second response.
"Why is this? That which the Tathāgata calls 'endowment with all marks' is in fact not an endowment; it is merely designated as 'endowment with all marks.'"
The commentary states: This is the second interpretation.
Vasubandhu says: "The Tathāgata is not possessed of the various marks" refers to the thirty-two distinct marks.
"Non-attainment of perfection" means that it is not the case that the Dharma-body is perfected by way of undifferentiated characteristics.
"This is called the perfection of all marks" refers to external physical forms.

Asuṅga states: Although the *dharmakāya* is devoid of form and characteristics, it possesses the characteristic of the *dharmatā*; that is to say, the "characteristic" refers to the elegance of principle (*li*).

Within its external manifestation, there are likewise forms and characteristics; this is because, in order to enable sentient beings to attain this kind of perfection, it manifests the characteristic of having characteristics externally, based on the characteristic of the signless characteristic of internally realizing the true reality.
However, the characteristic of having characteristics is itself the characteristic of being without characteristics; this is called the perfection of all characteristics.
"Subhūti, you must not think that the Tathāgata has the thought: 'I shall preach some Dharma.'"
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this third section addresses a doubt regarding the second passage.
Specifically, there is a doubt as follows:
"If the Tathāgata’s perfection of the form-body (*rūpakāya*) cannot be perceived, and his perfection of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) cannot be perceived, how does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma?"
This is for the purpose of dispelling such doubts.
Within this, first, there is the command not to harbor doubt; second, the accusation of slandering the Buddha by others; and third, the final summary that establishes the point—this is the first.
The Buddha told Subhūti:
"Do not think that the Dharma-body Tathāgata has the thought, 'I shall have something to say. For the Buddha of the Dharma-body is fundamentally without thought, nor does he have anything to say."

Asuṅga states: "This fifth [body] exists for the sake of the perfection of speech; that is to say, it possesses verbal expression according to the capacities of those being transformed or as a retribution-body. The Dharma-body is profound and tranquil, without speech and without form."
Having personally realized the ineffable principle within, one is able to explain it to others; it is for the sake of enabling them to attain this that speech serves as a complete instrument.
"Do not entertain such thoughts. Why is this?"
"If anyone says, 'The Tathāgata has preached a Dharma,' they slander the Buddha, for they fail to understand what I have taught.
The commentary states: This is the second passage.
This means that if there were any dharma-body that preached the Dharma, one would be slandering both the Dharma and the Buddha, for [the true nature] is quiescent and beyond speech.
Question:
"If that is so, why did you previously state, 'The emanated and transformed [bodies] are not the true Buddha, nor are they the preachers of the Dharma'?"

Answer: "Because he attributes the merit to its source, he requires internal realization of the truth before speaking; as for what can be spoken externally, the Dharma-body is called 'non-speaking,' which is itself the true speaking."

Question: "For what reason does the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* state that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) teaches the dharma that is free from characteristics and free from words; the Reward-body (sambhogakāya) teaches the dharma of the ten stages and the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā); and the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) teaches the dharma of the three vehicles (tri-yāna)?"
"Based on this, the Dharma-body is also spoken of. He replied:

"There are two kinds of speaking: first, speaking through conditioned activity, which refers to speaking that has speech; second, speaking without conditioned activity, which refers to speaking that is without speech."
The former refers to the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), while the latter refers to the dharma body (*dharmakāya*).
The former is based on the teaching of "not speaking," whereas this is based on the teaching of "speaking"; therefore, they do not contradict one another.
What is meant by the Dharma-body teaching through non-teaching?
It refers to the fact that because sentient beings realize and penetrate the principle, they comprehend all things; this is called the teaching of the Dharma-body.
Just as one understands and penetrates upon hearing the teaching of the Dharma, it is therefore called "teaching."
"It is like a person who, whether speaking or remaining silent, causes others to understand; this is called 'preaching the Dharma.
Subhūti, as for one who preaches the Dharma, there is no dharma that can be preached; it is for this reason that it is called 'preaching the Dharma.'"
The commentary states: This is the third conclusion.
"The one who preaches the Dharma" refers to the general act of preaching the Dharma.
"There is no dharma that can be preached" means that within the ultimate truth, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be expressed.
This means that one must explain by reaching the realization that the thoroughly imagined nature is empty and non-existent; this is called teaching the Dharma.
If one clings to true suchness as being substantially existent and thus fails to teach, it is not teaching the Dharma.
As Asaṅga says: "The Reward Body and Transformation Body are said to have speech, while the Dharma Body has no speech;
if one were to say that the Dharma Body has speech just as the Reward and Transformation Bodies do, that would constitute slandering the Buddha-Dharma."
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha,
saying: “World-Honored One,
will there be any sentient beings in future ages who, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, will give rise to faith and confidence?”
The commentary states: This passage is cited from the *Śrāvastī* [Sūtra].
For Vasubandhu, this is the third text within the third section of doubts.
It refers to a doubt that arises as follows:
"If one says that it was spoken by the Buddhas, it is a teaching of non-speaking;
it does not depart from the Dharma-body, and it is likewise nothing at all. Who could have faith in such a profoundly deep realm of reality (dharmadhātu)?"
Regarding the resolution of this doubt, first is the question of Subhūti, followed by the answer of the Tathāgata;

this is the former. As Vasubandhu states, within the fulfillment of the sixth mind there are further six aspects: first, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); second, the right awakenings (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); third, the establishment of the great beneficial Dharma; fourth, the appropriation of the *dharmakāya*; fifth, non-abiding in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa; and sixth, the purity of conduct and dwelling. This is the first [of these].
The question means:

"When the Tathāgata was in the world, he taught with impartial compassion for the sake of sentient beings. If there are those who can hear this, give rise to mindfulness, attend to it according to principle, practice in accordance with the Dharma, and act in conformity with the Dharma, they shall attain Buddhahood."

In the five hundred years following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata, when various evil sentient beings hear this sutra being preached, will there be those who can give rise to faith and conceive the thought: "Is it as if the Buddha were still in the world?"
The Buddha replied, "There are. This is said to reveal that there are sentient beings capable of mindfulness; therefore, they are called "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
The Buddha said, "Subhūti!..."
"He is neither a sentient being nor is he not a sentient being.
The commentary states: Within this second response of the Buddha, there is first the thesis and second the explanation; this is the first.
"Those who are not sentient beings" refers to those icchantikas who lack the Buddha-nature;
"those who are not non-sentient beings" refers to those sentient beings who, having heard the Prajñāpāramitā, have resolved to attain Buddhahood.
As Asaṅga says: "They are not sentient beings because of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya);
they are not non-sentient beings because of the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya).
To speak of them as 'sentient beings, sentient beings' is to manifest and explain the ultimate truth, for it is both unique and consistent."
"Why is this? Subhūti!
As for 'sentient beings, sentient beings,' the Tathāgata has said they are not sentient beings; they are merely named 'sentient beings.'"
The commentary states: This is the explanation.
The initial mention of "sentient beings" refers to ordinary worldlings;
furthermore, the phrase "as for sentient beings" refers to those sentient beings who have awakened the bodhicitta and are engaged in spiritual practice.
"When the Tathāgata says 'not a sentient being,' he means it is not the icchantika—a being who lacks the Buddha-nature;
when he says 'sentient beings are called sentient beings,' he refers to those sentient beings who have resolved their minds [for enlightenment]."

The underlying intent here is as follows: those who give rise to faith in this sutra are precisely those sentient beings who have awakened the aspiration for enlightenment, who practice, and who attain Buddhahood; they are not sentient beings devoid of the Buddha-nature.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
When the Buddha attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, is it that there is nothing to be attained?"

The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that within this major section, the fourth doubt is refuted; this is the second of the two successive doubts within the second [section] of the sequential explanation.
Within this passage there are two doubts; this is the first.
A doubt is raised as follows:

"If a Tathāgata does not attain a single dharma and is thus called 'Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment,' how is it that he attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through a process of successive realizations, each higher than the last?"
In this passage there are two parts: first, Subhūti’s question; second, the Tathāgata’s extensive elucidation of its meaning. This is the former.
Regarding the phrase "Is it because of non-attainment?", the particle *ye* is an interrogative particle and not an indefinite pronoun.
He asked the Buddha directly: "Does the Tathāgata have nothing to attain?
This is why the Buddha immediately confirmed it.
Had he not asked with such certainty, but instead asked whether there was attainment or non-attainment, how could the Buddha have confirmed it so readily?
Therefore, the intent of the present question is: "Does the Buddha attain unsurpassed bodhi within the principle of *tathatā* (suchness)?

Asaṅga states that this refers to the second [aspect] among the perfections of the mind, which constitutes perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). This refers to the means of realization, the object of realization, the contemplative observation, and the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states: "Both awakening and the abandonment [of what is to be abandoned] are both termed 'awakening' (bodhi)";
and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To speak of wisdom and the locus of wisdom is to speak of both as 'prajñā'."

This means that because this text exists for the purpose of enabling sentient beings to sever the two obstacles and attain the two types of bodhi, it is said to be "for the sake of perfect enlightenment" (*samyaksambodhi*).
Within the text there are five sections: first, the manifestation of the term *anuttara*, which refers to supreme enlightenment, namely the Bodhi of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
second, the section below that manifests *samyaksambodhi*, which refers to perfect enlightenment, namely the Bodhi of the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
From "Because there is no self, person, etc. below, both of the two preceding points are established.
Within the first [of these], there is first the question and next the confirmation; this is the former.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Subhūti! In my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, there is not even the slightest dharma that can be apprehended; this is what is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The commentary states: This second seal asks whether one accords with reality.
It means that within the true principle, there is not even the slightest thing obtained as one has grasped it; this is called bodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti! This Dharma is equal, without high or low; this is called Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this constitutes the third extensive exposition of its meaning.
Within this, there are three parts: first, clarifying that there is neither increase nor decrease;
second, revealing that there is no distinction.
Below the phrase "cultivating all wholesome [dharmas]," the fulfillment of skillful means is revealed;
this is the first instance.
"This Dharma is equal" means that the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) neither increases nor decreases.

"Without high or low" means that conditioned phenomena involve acceptance and rejection, as Bodhisattvas in the ten stages attain superior untainted dharmas and abandon inferior ones; however, because unconditioned phenomena have no superiority or inferiority to be accepted or rejected, they are said to be "without high or low."
As Asanga says: "This reveals *samyaksambodhi*, which is to say, perfect universal knowledge (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
'This dharma is equal' means that all Buddhas together attain bodhi, for there is no superiority or inferiority in their wisdom."
"Without high or low" means that when all Buddhas manifest transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), they are equal across all categories, even to the extent that their lifespans are equal.

You say that "equality" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while "high and low" pertains to the reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation-body; this means that the reward-bodies of all Buddhas are equal, and the same applies to their transformation-bodies.
"By means of no-self, no person, no sentient being, and no life-span.
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this second [point] reveals non-differentiation.

This means that because all Buddhas' dharmas are free from the grasping of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-abhiniveśa*), their Dharma-bodies are equal and without distinction, whether superior or inferior.

As Asaṅga says: "From here below, the two [aspects] together establish the two [types of] enlightenment above. First, it establishes the *anuttara* Dharma-body enlightenment (*dharmakāya-bodhi*) mentioned above;
second, it establishes the *samyaksaṃbodhi* Reward-body enlightenment (*saṃbhogakāya-bodhi*) mentioned above. This first [point] may be understood."
"By practicing all wholesome dharmas, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this third [section] demonstrates the fulfillment of skillful means.
Within this, the first part is the actual exposition and the second is the conclusion; this is the former.

That is to say, by approaching spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), hearing the teachings, reflecting upon them, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, and engaging in practice that accords with the Dharma, one fulfills the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). Consequently, one realizes and attains the ultimate truth, which is called "accomplishing *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
Asuṅga says: "This establishes the aforementioned *samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Within this [section], there is first the actual establishment and second the concluding explanation; this is the former."
The previous statement that there is no self and so forth was intended to eliminate the attachment to existence;
the present statement that one should cultivate goodness is intended to shatter the attachment to emptiness.
Since both self and person are empty, one must dispel the deluded mind of the self.
Because dependent and perfected existence exist, one must preserve wholesome dharmas.
For if one studies only existence and not emptiness, deluded conceptualization will increase further;
if one studies only emptiness and not existence, true wisdom will have no cause to arise.

"Extinguish deluded thoughts at the gate of emptiness and give rise to the true mind at the repository of existence; by contemplating both emptiness and existence together, one then achieves the Middle Way. Subhūti!"
"What is called wholesome dharmas," the Tathāgata says, "is not actually wholesome dharmas; it is merely designated as 'wholesome dharmas.
The commentary states: This is the second passage.
"What is called wholesome dharmas" refers to the wholesome dharmas sought for the sake of awakening, or the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas, or those dharmas that accord with the untainted.
Regarding "the teaching of non-virtuous dharmas," these are not the tainted, arising-and-ceasing dharmas of evil or virtue;
regarding "these are called virtuous dharmas," these are supramundane virtues.
“Subhūti! If there were someone who took as a gift all the heaps of the seven treasures equal in measure to all the Sumeru kings within a trichiliocosm, and offered them as an act of giving;”
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that from this point downward, he refutes the doubts of the second sub-section.
Specifically, there is a doubt which says:
"If one attains bodhi by fulfilling all wholesome dharmas, then the dharmas being taught here cannot lead to the attainment of great bodhi."
"Why is this? Because the Dharma that is taught consists of indeterminate dharmas.
This means: since the expressive teachings consist of names, phrases, and phonemes, whose nature is indeterminate, how can hearing them give rise to wholesome states?
This is the doubt of those of the Hīnayāna.
Within the refutation of this doubt, there are two parts: first, the presentation of merits; second, the comparative evaluation of receiving and upholding [the precepts]. This is the former.
As Asaṅga says: "This is the third [section] within the 'Perfection of Mind,' for the purpose of establishing the Dharma of Great Benefit.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the clarification of the Dharma of Great Benefit; second, from the words 'You should not say' onwards, the manifestation of the sentient beings who are benefited."
At the beginning, the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*) is first presented; next, the benefit and merit are revealed through a comparative analysis of its upholding. This is the first [point]:

"If a person takes up, upholds, reads, recites, and explains to others even as little as a four-line verse from this *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the previously mentioned merit will not equal one hundredth part of it, nor one thousandth, ten-thousandth, or hundred-thousandth part; indeed, it cannot be reached by any calculation or analogy."
The commentary states: Vasubandhu says that this second section compares [the merit of] receiving and upholding [the precepts].
This sutra is somewhat abbreviated; other versions differ from this one.

Vasubandhu says: although this dharma is said to be indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it can bring about bodhi; for if one were to distance oneself from the dharma thus taught, one could not attain great bodhi, as this dharma can serve as the cause for bodhi.
Furthermore, to say that it is indeterminate is incorrect.

"Your dharma is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), whereas my dharma is wholesome (*kuśala*). This explanation follows the tenets of that [opponent's] school; according to them, the Buddha’s words are wholesome.

Furthermore, according to the meaning of the Mahāyāna, once Buddhahood is attained, sounds, names, and phrases are all wholesome. Therefore, at the very moment one receives and upholds [this teaching], it becomes a vast cause for Bodhi. Consequently, it surpasses the giving of immeasurable other treasures; this directly refutes the aforementioned doubt.

Regarding the phrase "not even one percent" and so forth, the masters of the treatises identify four kinds of comparative superiority: first, superiority in number; second, superiority in power; third, superiority through lack of resemblance; and fourth, superiority in cause.

The commentary explains that "superiority in number" refers to calculating by means of numerical values. Specifically, the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) has sixty-two numbers, while the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* has one hundred and twenty cycles of numbers; furthermore, this region [of China] has fifteen, namely: one, ten, hundred, thousand, ten thousand, and so forth. By comparing through such numbers, the retributions of birth and death can all be fully known.
If one upholds this sutra, one shall attain all the merits of a Buddha; these cannot be measured by such numbers, and for this reason it is said that the number is supreme.

As for "superiority of power," it refers to the superiority of conceptual intention (*saṃkalpa*). That is to say, the worldly fruits of goodness—those of humans and devas—obtained through acts such as giving can be known through conceptual intention; however, the cause of this present receiving and upholding cannot be measured or calculated by conceptual intention.

Regarding "superiority through dissimilarity," this refers to the superiority of the analogy; while worldly fruits of merit can be illustrated by means of an analogy, the superior fruit obtained from the causes of receiving and upholding [the teaching] has no analogy by which it can be illustrated.
